rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, no heavy lifting until pain resolves, heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical therapy if pain persists despite NSAIDs; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise
Vascular claudication: calf pain, bicycling too; standing still relieves; weak pulses alone don't exclude stenosis

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates
Shopping-cart sign; pulses usually preserved; MRI confirms

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.scope: Non-small cell, small cell, paraneoplastic syndromes, Pancoast, screening
lung-cancer.core: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a suspicious lung lesion requires tissue diagnosis and staging before treatment selection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens, prior thoracic radiation; adenocarcinoma also occurs in never-smokers
Leading cause of cancer death in men and women; smoking is the predominant risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Recurrent focal pneumonia, hoarseness, unexplained pleural effusion
★ **Pancoast tumor**: shoulder/ulnar-arm pain + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
SVC obstruction: facial swelling, neck-vein distention; cord compression or airway compromise requires urgent action
Painful long-bone periostitis ± clubbing/joint swelling → **hypertrophic osteoarthropathy**, a lung cancer complication

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bronchogenic malignant transformation → local invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous metastasis
Ectopic hormone production and immune cross-reactivity cause paraneoplastic syndromes
Central endobronchial tumor → bronchial obstruction → **post-obstructive pneumonia**, atelectasis, lobar collapse
Ectopic **ACTH** (polypeptide; cortisol excess secondary) → hyperpigmentation, hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis, proximal weakness

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious finding → **contrast chest CT**; biopsy easiest site that establishes highest stage
Central lesion/nodes → bronchoscopy/EBUS; peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; effusion → cytology
PET/CT for extracranial staging, brain MRI for selected stages/small-cell disease; pulmonary function before resection
Molecular profiling and PD-L1 guide advanced NSCLC treatment; suspicious nodes often require pathologic staging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early operable NSCLC → **surgical resection + nodal evaluation**; inoperable localized → stereotactic radiation
Locally advanced NSCLC → combined systemic treatment/radiation ± surgery in selected patients
Metastatic NSCLC → biomarker-directed agents or immunotherapy/chemotherapy
★ Small-cell → **platinum + etoposide**, stage-dependent radiation/immunotherapy; surgery rarely used
SVC syndrome from small-cell → urgent **chemotherapy** ± radiation; stent if severe; diuretics not definitive

rows.label: Complications
items: Brain/bone/adrenal/liver metastases, malignant effusion, thrombosis, respiratory failure
Radiation pneumonitis; checkpoint inhibitors → immune pneumonitis/endocrinopathies

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **annual low-dose CT**, age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoking or quit <15 years
Stop after 15 quit-years or limited curative candidacy; **ACS omits quit-time restriction**
Smoking cessation and radon mitigation; chest radiographs do not substitute for screening CT

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal granuloma: microbiologic evidence; PET uptake not specific for cancer
Hamartoma: fat/popcorn calcification; pneumonia: clinical/radiographic response to antibiotics

lung-cancer.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2021](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening), [ACS 2023 guideline](https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.3322/caac.21811); treatment: established stage-based framework.

measures-of-association.name: Measures of association
measures-of-association.scope: Relative risk (RR), odds ratio (OR), attributable risk (AR), absolute risk reduction (ARR), number needed to treat (NNT), number needed to harm (NNH), hazard ratio
measures-of-association.core: Relative measures describe proportional associations; absolute measures incorporate baseline risk and determine treatment benefit or harm.

rows.label: Definition
items: CER = control event rate; EER = experimental event rate
Two-by-two table: exposed events/non-events a/b; unexposed events/non-events c/d
Relative risk reduction (RRR; vaccine efficacy) = (CER − EER)/CER = 1 − RR

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ Ratio null = **1**; risk-difference null = **0**
★ Hazard ratio compares instantaneous event rates over time; not cumulative risk ratio
NNT/NNH require specified outcome and follow-up duration; always round up

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ RR: cohort/RCT; OR: case-control and logistic regression
Attributable risk: excess incidence among exposed attributable to exposure, assuming causality
HR: survival analysis with censoring; constant interpretation assumes proportional hazards

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Use proportions, not percentage numbers, in reciprocal calculations
OR approximates RR only with rare outcomes; common outcomes exaggerate relative association
Association alone cannot establish causality; confounding can distort every measure

measures-of-association.evidence: Statistical definitions; no clinical guideline involved.

meckel-diverticulum.name: Meckel diverticulum
meckel-diverticulum.scope: Persistent vitelline duct, ectopic gastric mucosa, painless lower GI bleeding, technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, intussusception, surgical resection
meckel-diverticulum.core: A congenital ileal remnant can present with childhood intestinal bleeding, obstruction, or appendicitis-like inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Persistent **vitelline/omphalomesenteric duct**; congenital lesion, symptomatic disease more common in boys
Ectopic gastric tissue increases bleeding; complications often arise in childhood, but possible at any age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painless maroon or bright-red rectal bleeding** in an otherwise well child
Colicky pain, vomiting or obstruction when serving as an intussusception lead point
Diverticulitis → fever, RLQ pain and tenderness; perforation produces peritoneal signs
Large-volume blood loss → pallor, tachycardia or shock; benign abdominal examination does not ensure mild disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: True diverticulum contains all bowel-wall layers, usually antimesenteric distal ileum
Acid secretion from heterotopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileal lining

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected bleeding Meckel → **technetium-99m pertechnetate scan**, detects gastric mucosa
Negative scan does not exclude lesion without sufficient ectopic tissue; pediatric sensitivity exceeds adult sensitivity
Ultrasound if intussusception suspected; CT for inflammatory/obstructive presentations or alternative diagnoses
CBC, type/crossmatch for substantial bleeding; endoscopic studies may be unrevealing because lesion lies beyond routine reach

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Brisk bleeding/shock → **IV access, crystalloid/blood**, urgent pediatric/surgical consultation
★ Symptomatic lesion → **diverticulectomy or segmental ileal resection**, including adjacent ulcerated bowel
Perforation/peritonitis → broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent operation; obstruction → NPO and decompression
Incidentally found asymptomatic lesion → individualized surgical decision based on risk and operative context

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent hemorrhage and anemia, intussusception, volvulus around fibrous band, bowel ischemia
Diverticulitis or perforation; postoperative adhesions can cause later small-bowel obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Juvenile polyp: painless bleeding but intraluminal colonic lesion on colonoscopy
Anal fissure: painful stooling with surface streaks; peptic bleeding: upper-GI source

meckel-diverticulum.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.name: Medical errors and patient safety
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.scope: Near miss, adverse event, error disclosure, root cause analysis, structured sign-outs and handoffs
medical-errors-and-patient-safety.core: Protect the patient first, disclose errors honestly, and redesign systems to reduce recurrence.

rows.label: Principle
items: Just culture: distinguish human error, risky shortcuts, and reckless conduct
Psychological safety enables reporting; accountability and system improvement can coexist
Effective communication: bedside verbal handoff with patient → real-time feedback, shared mental model

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Stabilize and mitigate harm**, notify supervising clinician, preserve relevant clinical information
★ Disclose facts, consequences, **apology**, treatment/prevention plans; update uncertainties
★ Report through institutional safety system; document clinical facts and disclosure in medical record

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid concealment, altered records, premature blame, or speculation about causation
Do not rely on education alone when workflow permits predictable repeated errors
Do not trust result delivery alone (fax, mail); **test-tracking log** verifies receipt, review, follow-up

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Reckless impairment/dangerous conduct → remove from unsafe duties; institutional escalation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Root cause analysis**: retrospective system investigation; identify multiple contributors
Failure mode and effects analysis: prospective hazard assessment before harm
Handoff: standardized I-PASS/SBAR, pending tasks, contingency plans, receiver synthesis/read-back

table.title: Event classification
rows: Unanticipated death/serious harm/life-saving rescue; prompts RCA
Upstream scheduling/staffing flaw; fix system, not individual

medical-errors-and-patient-safety.evidence: Not checked online; established patient-safety terminology and ethical disclosure principles.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adults: **S. pneumoniae** most common; seeded by pneumonia, otitis, sinusitis, CSF leak, asplenia
Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; advanced HIV/transplant/chemotherapy → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: subacute, high opening pressure ± CN VI palsy, CSF antigen; TB studies if lymphocytic, low glucose

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal contacts within 7 days of onset → **rifampin or ceftriaxone**; droplet isolation until 24 hours treated
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss
Lithotomy/hip hyperflexion → **femoral** under inguinal ligament; stirrup at fibular head → foot drop
Antecubital hematoma after venipuncture → **median at elbow**; hook of hamate fracture → ulnar in Guyon canal

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex
Supraspinatus/infraspinatus atrophy, sensation intact, overhead athlete → **suprascapular** entrapment
Medial plantar laceration → medial toe hyperextension; superficial radial → dorsal web numbness, no wrist drop

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Ulnar hand intrinsics; forearm spared; wrist Tinel
Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

multiple-myeloma.name: Multiple myeloma
multiple-myeloma.scope: CRAB features (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, bone lytic lesions), SPEP/UPEP M-spike, serum free light chains, bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells), MGUS, smoldering myeloma
multiple-myeloma.core: A clonal plasma-cell malignancy causes monoclonal protein production and organ damage; modern biomarkers can establish treatment-requiring disease before symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, Black ancestry, male sex, preexisting MGUS; usually no identifiable preventable exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **CRAB**: hypercalcemia, renal impairment, anemia, lytic bone lesions
Back/rib pain, pathologic fracture, recurrent bacterial infection, high total protein, rouleaux
Acute weakness/back pain → cord compression; proteinuria or restrictive cardiomyopathy → consider AL amyloid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow expansion suppresses blood formation; osteoclast activation without osteoblast response causes bone destruction
Light chains injure renal tubules; low polyclonal immunoglobulins → **encapsulated bacteria**, e.g., pneumococcus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **SPEP/immunofixation + free light chains**, urine studies; light-chain disease may lack serum spike
★ **Bone marrow biopsy** quantifies clonal plasma cells; whole-body low-dose CT/MRI assesses bone disease
Active disease: ≥10% clonal marrow cells/plasmacytoma plus attributable CRAB or myeloma-defining biomarker
SLiM: marrow ≥60%; involved/uninvolved FLC ratio ≥100 with involved FLC ≥100 mg/L
MRI >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm defines active disease; bone scan may miss lytic lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Bortezomib-based combination** ± daratumumab/lenalidomide/dexamethasone; selected patients → autologous transplant
Hypercalcemia → saline plus antiresorptive; AKI → hydration, avoid NSAIDs/contrast and rapidly reduce light chains
Cord compression → dexamethasone and urgent MRI/radiation or surgery; treat infections promptly
MGUS/smoldering disease generally monitored; high-risk smoldering disease merits specialist assessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Cast nephropathy, vertebral collapse, hyperviscosity, AL amyloidosis; treatment-related neuropathy, infections and thrombosis
Urine dipstick detects albumin, misses light chains; negative dipstick does not exclude cast nephropathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccines, bisphosphonates; proteasome inhibitors → antiviral prophylaxis; immunomodulators → thromboprophylaxis by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Metastatic carcinoma: destructive lesions without clonal plasma-cell findings
Waldenström macroglobulinemia: IgM, hyperviscosity/lymphadenopathy, usually no lytic lesions

multiple-myeloma.evidence: Criteria checked 2026-10-30: [IMWG diagnostic criteria](https://www.myeloma.org/newly-diagnosed/multiple-myeloma-diagnostic-criteria); treatment: established generalist teaching.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, **Northern European ancestry**, family history; EBV, smoking, low vitamin D

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular loss, poor color vision, afferent pupillary defect, often normal fundus
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired ipsilateral adduction, contralateral abducting nystagmus; convergence intact
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse/optic neuritis → **high-dose IV methylprednisolone**, not low-dose prednisone; refractory → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

myelodysplastic-syndromes.name: Myelodysplastic syndromes
myelodysplastic-syndromes.scope: Cytopenias, macrocytic anemia, dysplastic neutrophils (Pelger-Huet anomaly), bone marrow biopsy, cytogenetics, progression to acute myeloid leukemia, transfusions
myelodysplastic-syndromes.core: Persistent unexplained cytopenias with an often cellular but ineffective marrow suggest a clonal myeloid neoplasm rather than simple nutrient deficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age; prior alkylating chemotherapy, topoisomerase inhibitors, radiation or benzene exposure
Usually acquired de novo; prior cytotoxic exposure raises concern for treatment-related myeloid neoplasm

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Macrocytic anemia with additional cytopenias**, despite adequate B12/folate
Fatigue/dyspnea, recurrent infections, bruising or mucosal bleeding; some cases discovered on routine CBC
Smear: hypogranular neutrophils, bilobed **pseudo-Pelger-Huët** nuclei, abnormal platelets
Circulating blasts or rapidly worsening counts → high-risk disease/transformation concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Clonal stem-cell abnormalities produce dysplastic maturation and intramedullary cell death
Peripheral cell scarcity despite commonly hypercellular marrow; selected cases hypocellular

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Exclude reversible causes → **bone marrow aspirate/biopsy with cytogenetics** and molecular testing
CBC, reticulocytes, smear, B12/folate, copper and iron assessment; review drugs/alcohol
≥10% dysplasia in a lineage or defining genetic findings supports diagnosis after excluding mimics
★ Usually **<20% blasts**; ≥20% generally AML, with genetic classification exceptions
Risk score combines blasts, cytogenetics/mutations and cytopenias; guides treatment intensity

rows.label: Tx
items: Symptomatic anemia → RBC transfusions; selected lower-risk anemia → erythropoiesis-stimulating agent or luspatercept
Isolated del(5q), lower-risk transfusion-dependent anemia → lenalidomide
★ Higher-risk disease → **azacitidine or decitabine**; fit candidates → allogeneic stem-cell transplant
Platelets for severe bleeding/thrombocytopenia; febrile neutropenia → prompt IV cefepime
Repeated transfusions with substantial overload → consider iron chelation in suitable long-surviving patients

rows.label: Complications
items: AML progression, serious infections, hemorrhage; transfusion iron overload and alloimmunization
Hypomethylating treatment initially worsens cytopenias; transplant → graft-versus-host disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12/folate deficiency: hypersegmented neutrophils, biochemical deficiency and response to replacement
Copper deficiency: cytopenias/dysplasia with zinc excess or malabsorption; reversible with copper

table.title: Morphologic terms
rows: Inherited hyposegmentation without acquired marrow failure

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established neonatal surgical teaching.

nephrotic-syndrome.name: Nephrotic syndrome
nephrotic-syndrome.scope: Minimal change, FSGS, membranous, diabetic nephropathy; thrombosis and hyperlipidemia
nephrotic-syndrome.core: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema indicates nephrotic syndrome; assess the cause and complications before choosing immunosuppression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, obesity, HIV, hepatitis B/C, autoimmune disease, malignancy and selected medications
Children favor minimal change; obesity, HIV, heroin or reduced nephron mass can cause secondary FSGS

rows.label: Clues
items: Periorbital/dependent edema, foamy urine, weight gain; severe cases → anasarca or effusions
Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria, oval fat bodies/fatty casts; urine sediment often otherwise bland
★ Sudden flank pain, hematuria or falling filtration → **renal vein thrombosis**
Low effective volume may coexist with overload; edema gone + orthostasis/oliguria on diuretic → **overdiuresis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Podocyte barrier damage leaks albumin; sodium retention and low oncotic pressure promote edema
Urinary loss of anticoagulants and immunoglobulins increases thrombosis and infection risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adult protein **>3.5 g/day** or equivalent spot protein/creatinine ratio; serum albumin and lipid profile
Urinalysis/microscopy, renal function, HbA1c; targeted HIV, HBV/HCV, ANA/complement and monoclonal-protein studies
★ Most unexplained adult cases → **kidney biopsy**; classic childhood minimal change often treated empirically
Anti-PLA2R supports primary membranous disease; assess secondary causes and age-based cancer screening
Diabetes with retinopathy, gradually rising albuminuria → likely diabetic nephropathy; atypical features → consider biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Salt restriction, **loop diuretic**, ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; monitor perfusion and K
Eligible CKD → SGLT2 inhibitor; treat diabetes/infection or remove causative drug
Minimal change/primary FSGS → glucocorticoids; secondary FSGS → cause-directed/supportive treatment, not routine steroids
Membranous disease → risk-stratified observation versus rituximab or other immunosuppression
★ Confirmed thrombosis → anticoagulate; preventive anticoagulation individualized by albumin, pathology and bleeding risk

rows.label: Complications
items: DVT/PE, renal vein thrombosis, cellulitis/peritonitis, AKI, accelerated atherosclerosis
Progressive glomerular scarring can lead to kidney failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccinate, control BP/glycemia, avoid NSAIDs; monitor treatment toxicity and recurrent proteinuria

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephritic syndrome: dysmorphic RBCs/casts, hypertension, inflammatory sediment
Cirrhosis: low albumin without nephrotic protein loss

table.title: Classic pathology
rows: Diffuse foot-process effacement; normal light microscopy

nephrotic-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching and risk-based treatment principles.

neural-tube-defects.name: Neural tube defects
neural-tube-defects.scope: Anencephaly, spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, Chiari II malformation, maternal serum AFP, amniotic acetylcholinesterase, lemon and banana signs, folic acid prevention
neural-tube-defects.core: Neural tube closure failure by approximately 4 weeks after conception produces cranial or spinal defects; prevention must begin before pregnancy recognition.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Low folate, prior affected pregnancy, maternal diabetes/obesity, valproate/carbamazepine, early-pregnancy hyperthermia

rows.label: Clues
items: Midline lumbosacral sac, lower-limb weakness, absent reflexes, bladder dysfunction with neural involvement
★ **Lemon skull and banana cerebellum** on fetal ultrasound suggest open spina bifida/Chiari II
Occult lesions: hair tuft, atypical deep dimple, hemangioma; normal skin does not guarantee normal cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Failed neurulation leaves neural tissue unprotected; CSF leakage contributes to hindbrain herniation
Folate supports nucleotide synthesis during rapid embryonic cell division

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal serum **AFP at 15–22 weeks**; elevation → verify dating/number, detailed ultrasound
Open defects elevate AFP; closed occulta may not; cfDNA does not screen neural tube defects
★ Uncertain imaging → amniotic fluid **AFP and acetylcholinesterase**; target anatomy scan at 18–22 weeks
Postnatal spinal ultrasound in young infant or MRI for suspected occult dysraphism/tethered cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open spinal lesion: **prone positioning, sterile saline dressing**, avoid pressure/contamination; neonatal neurosurgery
Early closure; assess hydrocephalus, renal function and bladder emptying; intermittent catheterization when neurogenic
Selected prenatal myelomeningocele repair can improve motor outcomes/reduce shunting, with maternal and prematurity risks
Anencephaly → counseling, pregnancy options, and palliative neonatal care; no curative treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Hydrocephalus (Chiari II obstructs CSF), meningitis, orthopedic deformities, neurogenic bowel/bladder, recurrent UTI, kidney injury
Tethered cord may cause progressive weakness or continence changes during growth
Osteopenic insensate legs: new swelling → **X-ray** for occult fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Folic acid 400–800 µg/day** before conception through early pregnancy for average risk
Prior NTD pregnancy → **4 mg/day**, starting ≥1 month before conception through first 3 months
Optimize diabetes, review antiseizure drugs before pregnancy; avoid prolonged overheating

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sacrococcygeal teratoma: solid/cystic mass, not exposed neural placode
Abdominal wall defect: elevated AFP but bowel outside abdomen on ultrasound

table.title: Lesions
rows: Meninges/CSF herniate; cord remains within canal

neural-tube-defects.evidence: Folate checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/folic-acid/hcp/clinical-overview/), [USPSTF 2023](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/document/ClinicalSummaryFinal/folic-acid-for-the-prevention-of-neural-tube-defects-preventive-medication); remaining content established teaching.

neutropenia.name: Neutropenia
neutropenia.scope: Benign ethnic neutropenia (Duffy-null), drug-induced neutropenia, febrile neutropenia, autoimmune neutropenia, ANC thresholds, evaluation and management
neutropenia.core: Infection risk tracks the depth and duration of neutrophil depletion; fever with severe neutropenia is an antibiotic emergency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cytotoxic chemotherapy, marrow malignancy, viral infection, autoimmune disease, B12/folate/copper deficiency
Clozapine, methimazole, propylthiouracil, TMP–SMX and other drugs can cause agranulocytosis
Duffy-null associated neutrophil counts: stable isolated reduction without increased infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Oral ulcers, gingivitis, recurrent bacterial/fungal infections; inflammatory signs and pus may be absent
Cyclic mouth ulcers/infections suggest cyclic neutropenia; multiple cytopenias suggest marrow disease
Drug-associated fever or sore throat → urgent CBC, especially with antithyroid drugs

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced marrow production, peripheral destruction or splenic sequestration lowers circulating neutrophils
Mucosal barrier injury plus impaired innate defense permits rapid invasive bacterial infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ANC = WBC × (% neutrophils + bands)/100**; repeat CBC with differential and smear
Mild: 1000–1500/µL; moderate: 500–1000; **severe <500**; profound <100
★ Febrile neutropenia: **≥38.3°C once or ≥38.0°C for ≥1 hour**, ANC <500 or expected decline
Obtain peripheral/line blood cultures, targeted cultures and imaging without delaying antibiotics
Persistent unexplained severe counts, abnormal smear or other cytopenias → marrow evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Febrile severe neutropenia → **IV cefepime**, piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem promptly
Add vancomycin for shock, suspected line/skin infection, pneumonia or documented resistant gram-positive infection
★ Stop culprit drug; G-CSF for selected severe/drug-related cases and high-risk chemotherapy settings
Carefully selected low-risk stable patients → oral ciprofloxacin + amoxicillin–clavulanate with reliable close follow-up
High-risk persistent fever 4–7 days → fungal evaluation and empiric **caspofungin**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pseudomonas sepsis, invasive candidiasis/aspergillosis, neutropenic enterocolitis; avoid rectal instrumentation
**Ecthyma gangrenosum**: bulla → painless black necrotic ulcer, Pseudomonas bacteremia; antipseudomonal drug, not steroids

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hand hygiene, oral care; selected prolonged profound neutropenia → antibacterial/antifungal prophylaxis
Stable Duffy-null pattern → reassurance after excluding other causes; no unnecessary G-CSF

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphopenia: opportunistic infection risk with preserved ANC
Acute leukemia: blasts and additional cytopenias

normal-and-abnormal-labor.name: Normal and abnormal labor
normal-and-abnormal-labor.scope: Latent vs active first stage, second stage, active phase protraction and arrest (oxytocin, cesarean), false labor (Braxton Hicks), operative vaginal delivery, labor induction
normal-and-abnormal-labor.core: True labor produces progressive cervical change; dystocia management depends on stage, contraction adequacy, fetal status, and descent.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Nulliparity, obesity, fetal macrosomia, malposition, cephalopelvic disproportion, inadequate uterine contractions

rows.label: Clues
items: Assess membrane status, presentation, fetal heart tracing, serial dilation, station, and maternal vital signs
★ Tachysystole: **>5 contractions/10 minutes**, averaged over 30 minutes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysfunctional powers, passenger, or passage → delayed dilation or descent

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active arrest requires ruptured membranes: no change after **4 hours adequate** or 6 hours inadequate contractions
Adequate: ≥200 Montevideo units (summed mm Hg/10 minutes); IUPC when external assessment insufficient
Prolonged pushing: >3 hours nulliparous, >2 hours multiparous; individualize by descent and fetal status
Failed induction requires ≥12–18 hours oxytocin after ROM; slow latent phase alone does not mandate cesarean
Presenting part unpalpable → **ultrasound** for lie/presentation before amniotomy; floating part → cord prolapse risk

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Protraction (<1 cm/2 hours) with weak contractions → **oxytocin**, amniotomy; established active arrest → cesarean
Tachysystole → stop oxytocin, lateral positioning; persistent fetal compromise → terbutaline, expedited delivery
★ Operative birth: full dilation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, known position, skilled operator; failed → cesarean
Unfavorable cervix → balloon or prostaglandin ripening, then oxytocin; avoid misoprostol after prior cesarean
Labor pain → **epidural** most effective first-stage; pudendal block covers second stage only

rows.label: Complications
items: Maternal infection, hemorrhage, exhaustion; neonatal hypoxia
Forceps/vacuum → lacerations, scalp injury; vacuum → subgaleal hemorrhage, avoid <34 weeks or face presentation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Induce for maternal/fetal indications or offer elective induction from 39 weeks; no elective earlier delivery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: irregular, self-resolving, no cervical change → reassurance; GBS prophylaxis only in true labor/rupture
Obstructed labor: strong contractions, no progress; CPD (macrosomia), achondroplastic pelvis, transverse lie → **cesarean**, not oxytocin
Shoulder dystocia: head delivered, shoulders impacted; failed head descent at full dilation → CPD

table.title: Stages
rows: 6–10 cm; older exams may use ≥5 cm

nutritional-deficiencies.name: Nutritional deficiencies
nutritional-deficiencies.scope: Vegan diet nutrient risks, tea-and-toast diet, vitamin and mineral supplementation, clinical manifestations
nutritional-deficiencies.core: Restricted intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements produce characteristic mucocutaneous, neurologic, hematologic, and skeletal findings; identify the missing nutrient and its cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupplemented vegan diet: B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D, iodine, zinc risks
Tea-and-toast diet, alcohol misuse, food insecurity, restrictive eating, institutionalization
Bariatric surgery, pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, bowel disease → specific or fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor wound healing, bruising, oral changes, neuropathy, bone pain; mixed deficiencies commonly coexist
★ **Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia** in malnutrition → thiamine deficiency; complete triad often absent
Night blindness → vitamin A; bleeding with prolonged PT → vitamin K
Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia → niacin; periorificial/acral dermatitis, alopecia, dysgeusia → zinc (TPN, penicillamine)

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient cofactors impair energy metabolism, collagen formation, hematopoiesis, or mineralization
Low intake differs from malabsorption: replacement route and lasting supplementation must match the mechanism
Vitamin D deficiency → ↓calcium absorption → **secondary hyperparathyroidism**: normal calcium at bone's expense

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Diet and supplement history**, weight trend, oral/skin/neurologic examination; assess GI disease
CBC/ferritin, B12 ± methylmalonic acid, 25-OH vitamin D chosen by findings; avoid indiscriminate panels
Albumin is altered by inflammation/fluid status; not a stand-alone nutrition diagnostic test
Severely undernourished → baseline phosphate, Mg, K before nutritional rehabilitation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected Wernicke syndrome → **parenteral thiamine promptly**; do not await laboratory confirmation
B12 deficiency with neurologic signs/malabsorption → parenteral replacement; folate only after B12 assessment
Vitamin D/calcium for deficient intake or osteomalacia; iron replacement with evaluation for blood loss
Vitamin C for scurvy; oral balanced nutrition plus cause-directed supplementation and dietitian support
★ Severe malnutrition → **slow refeeding + thiamine**, close phosphate/K/Mg monitoring and replacement

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible B12 neurologic injury, fractures, anemia, infection susceptibility
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, respiratory failure; excess vitamin A → hepatotoxicity/teratogenicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vegans → **reliable B12 supplementation**; fortified foods, calcium/vitamin D and iodine adequacy
Diversified diet, food access support, lifelong bariatric follow-up; avoid megadose supplementation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Scurvy versus vasculitis: perifollicular hemorrhage/corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, restricted produce intake
Hypothyroidism: fatigue and macrocytosis with elevated TSH

nutritional-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established nutritional deficiency and refeeding principles.

opioid-toxicity.name: Opioid toxicity
opioid-toxicity.scope: Opioid toxidrome, naloxone administration and titration, observation period, precipitated withdrawal
opioid-toxicity.core: Depressed consciousness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils after opioid exposure; ventilation takes priority over full awakening.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fentanyl or heroin exposure, dose escalation, renal dysfunction, long-acting opioids
Alcohol/benzodiazepine co-ingestion; lost tolerance after detoxification, hospitalization, or incarceration

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Bradypnea or apnea** with hypoxemia; reduced bowel sounds, bradycardia, hypotension
Miosis may be absent with severe hypoxia or co-ingestion; needle marks are not required
Pulmonary edema, aspiration, hypothermia, prolonged immobilization may accompany overdose
Chronic use: daytime sleepiness, constipation, apathy, falling grades, miosis, slow breathing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mu-receptor activation suppresses medullary ventilatory response to CO2
Naloxone competitively reverses opioid effects but often wears off before the causative opioid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bedside glucose, pulse oximetry, capnography; do not await toxicology
Urine opiate immunoassay detects morphine/heroin/codeine; may miss fentanyl, methadone, and oxycodone
ECG for methadone-associated QT prolongation; acetaminophen level with uncertain combination-product ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Open airway, **bag-mask ventilation**, oxygen; intubate if ventilation cannot be maintained
★ **Naloxone** IV titrated to adequate breathing; intranasal/IM route if IV unavailable
Dependent but breathing: start low; apnea/no response: prompt larger/repeated doses, especially fentanyl analogs
Repeated recurrence → naloxone infusion; coma despite repeated doses → evaluate additional causes
Short-acting reversal: observe ≥4 hours after last naloxone; long-acting/recurrent sedation → prolonged monitoring/admission

rows.label: Complications
items: Anoxic brain injury, aspiration pneumonia, rhabdomyolysis, compartment syndrome
Precipitated withdrawal: agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, tachycardia; rare pulmonary edema after reversal

rows.label: Prevention
items: Take-home naloxone, overdose-response training, avoid sedative combinations; offer buprenorphine and addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pontine hemorrhage: focal neurologic findings, no meaningful naloxone response
Clonidine poisoning: marked bradycardia with similar pupils
Sedative overdose: usually normal pupils; incomplete naloxone response

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.scope: Epithelial ovarian carcinoma, CA-125, pelvic ultrasound, peritoneal carcinomatosis, germ cell tumors, sex cord-stromal tumors, surgical staging and cytoreduction, platinum-based chemotherapy
ovarian-cancer.core: Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic symptoms, or an adnexal mass—especially after menopause—requires evaluation for an often late-presenting malignancy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Increasing age, nulliparity, BRCA1/2 or Lynch syndrome; family history of breast/ovarian cancer
Endometriosis associated with clear-cell/endometrioid subtypes; pregnancy and combined contraceptives reduce epithelial risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Older patient + ascites, large/fixed pelvic mass, weight loss, pleural effusion, obstruction → **epithelial** carcinoma
Young patient with rapidly enlarging mass → germ cell tumor; estrogen/androgen effects → stromal tumor
Postmenopausal bleeding with adnexal mass → consider estrogen-secreting granulosa tumor and endometrial disease
★ **Palpable ovary after menopause** → abnormal (ovaries atrophy); pelvic ultrasound

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Many high-grade serous tumors arise in distal fallopian tube epithelium
Transcoelomic seeding produces peritoneal/omental disease; hormone secretion depends on tumor lineage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Transvaginal ultrasound** first; solid components, papillary projections, vascularity, ascites increase suspicion
★ **CA-125** supports risk assessment/monitoring, not diagnosis or average-risk screening
Young/complex mass → β-hCG, AFP, LDH; suspected stromal tumor → inhibin/sex hormones
Suspected malignancy → CT abdomen/pelvis/chest and gynecologic oncology; definitive histology and staging usually surgical
Isolated resectable mass → avoid aspiration; advanced disease → biopsy before neoadjuvant chemotherapy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Epithelial carcinoma → **surgical staging/cytoreduction + carboplatin/paclitaxel** according to stage
Poor upfront surgical candidate → tissue confirmation, neoadjuvant platinum chemotherapy, interval cytoreduction
Germ cell malignancy → fertility-sparing surgery when feasible; stage IA dysgerminoma may avoid chemotherapy
Higher-risk germ cell tumors → bleomycin/etoposide/cisplatin
Selected BRCA/HRD-associated disease → PARP-inhibitor maintenance after platinum response

rows.label: Complications
items: Peritoneal carcinomatosis, ascites, malignant obstruction, VTE; chemotherapy neuropathy/myelosuppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **No routine CA-125/ultrasound screening** in asymptomatic average-risk patients
Genetic counseling/testing; hereditary high-risk patients → discuss risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endometrioma: cyclic pain, ground-glass ultrasound; CA-125 can rise
Meigs syndrome: benign ovarian fibroma plus ascites/pleural effusion; no peritoneal implants

table.title: Tumor markers
rows: Often bilateral; psammoma bodies; WT1+, p53 abnormal

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may show **double-duct** (bile + pancreatic) dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen
Massive watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria, flushing

pancreatic-cancer.evidence: Not checked online; established pancreatic oncology teaching.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.scope: Acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis, exocrine and endocrine insufficiency
pancreatitis.core: Epigastric pain radiating to the back with pancreatic inflammation may be acute; repeated injury produces irreversible chronic insufficiency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gallstones (prior postprandial biliary colic), heavy alcohol, triglycerides >1,000 mg/dL, ERCP, hypercalcemia, medications
Chronic: prolonged alcohol/tobacco exposure, genetic disease, duct obstruction, autoimmune disease
Blunt abdominal trauma + epigastric mass/raised enzymes → contrast CT for pancreatic/duodenal injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Severe constant pain, vomiting, tenderness, ileus; chronic disease adds steatorrhea and weight loss
★ **Hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria, persistent SIRS** → early monitored/ICU assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature intrapancreatic enzyme activation → autodigestion and systemic inflammation
Chronic fibrosis destroys acinar/islet tissue: ↓insulin, ↓glucagon, normal insulin sensitivity; lipase may normalize

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Acute diagnosis: **2 of 3**—typical pain, lipase or amylase ≥3× ULN, characteristic imaging
RUQ ultrasound evaluates gallstones; triglycerides, calcium, liver tests identify cause
Contrast CT: diagnostic doubt, high fever/marked leukocytosis (necrosis?), deterioration, no improvement by 48–72 hours; not routine early
Chronic: CT/MRCP shows calcification/duct changes; fecal elastase <200 supports exocrine insufficiency
Recurrent, no gallstones/alcohol → EUS or MRCP for ductal anatomy; older exam questions may expect ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute: **moderate lactated Ringer resuscitation**, reassessment, IV opioid analgesia, electrolyte correction; avoid overload
★ **Early oral low-fat feeding** by 48 hours if tolerated; else enteral; older exam questions may expect initial bowel rest
Biliary with cholangitis → urgent ERCP; mild gallstone disease → cholecystectomy before discharge
Uncomplicated/sterile: no antibiotics; infected necrosis: penetrating antibiotics, delayed step-up drainage/debridement
Chronic: stop alcohol/tobacco; pancrelipase, fat-soluble vitamins, pain control; islet-loss diabetes → **insulin**, not sulfonylureas

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, AKI, shock, hypocalcemia; necrosis, hemorrhage; **splenic vein thrombosis** → isolated gastric varices, normal liver
Pseudocyst after >4 weeks; infected collection, obstruction; chronic disease → pancreatic cancer and brittle diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Treat cause**: gallbladder removal, triglyceride control, avoid culprit drug and alcohol
Post-ERCP rectal indomethacin in eligible patients; selected pancreatic duct stenting

rows.label: Mimics
items: Perforated ulcer: rigid abdomen/free air
Mesenteric ischemia: pain-exam mismatch; MI: ischemic ECG/troponin pattern

table.title: Severity and collections
rows: Transient dysfunction ≤48 hours or local complication

parkinson-disease.name: Parkinson disease
parkinson-disease.scope: Cardinal motor symptoms (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability/pull test), nonmotor symptoms, dopamine agonists, levodopa-carbidopa, atypical parkinsonism (PSP, MSA)
parkinson-disease.core: Progressive asymmetric bradykinesia with characteristic motor signs and levodopa responsiveness suggests Parkinson disease; early atypical features prompt another diagnosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, family susceptibility, some pesticide exposures; most disease sporadic
Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics/metoclopramide cause secondary parkinsonism rather than idiopathic disease
MPTP (synthetic heroin contaminant) → rapid parkinsonism from nigral dopaminergic neuron destruction

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity**, reduced arm swing, shuffling gait
Freezing, micrographia, hypophonia; pull test reveals impaired postural recovery, typically later
Constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behavior disorder, depression and autonomic symptoms can precede motor disease
Early severe falls, gaze palsy, marked autonomic failure or poor treatment response → atypical syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Substantia nigra dopaminergic neuron loss; α-synuclein Lewy bodies
Reduced striatal dopamine disrupts basal ganglia motor regulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; bradykinesia plus resting tremor and/or rigidity
Brain MRI for atypical findings; dopamine transporter imaging if uncertain degenerative versus nondegenerative tremor
Review medications; assess cognition, orthostatic BP, gait and swallowing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Function-limiting motor symptoms → **carbidopa/levodopa**, preferred initial dopaminergic treatment
Pramipexole/ropinirole for selected younger patients; avoid with hallucinations, impulse-control problems or age >70
Wearing-off → adjust levodopa schedule, add MAO-B/COMT inhibitor; dyskinesia → amantadine
★ Exercise, PT/speech/swallow rehab; refractory fluctuations/tremor/dyskinesias → **deep brain stimulation**, pallidotomy
Psychosis → reduce provoking drugs; pimavanserin or selected quetiapine/clozapine, avoid potent dopamine blockers

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, dementia; medication → hallucinations, orthostasis, motor fluctuations/dyskinesias
Dopamine agonists → gambling/hypersexuality and sleep attacks; abrupt withdrawal → severe rigidity/hyperthermia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall-proof home, medication adherence, aspiration-risk assessment; no established primary neuroprotective treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Essential tremor: action/postural tremor without decrementing bradykinesia
Drug-induced: blocker exposure, often symmetric; normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, urinary/cognitive symptoms

table.title: Atypical parkinsonism
rows: Severe orthostasis/urinary dysfunction, possible cerebellar signs
Dementia before or within 1 year of parkinsonism

pediatric-exanthems.name: Pediatric exanthems
pediatric-exanthems.scope: Measles (rubeola), rubella (German measles), roseola infantum (HHV-6), erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19 fifth disease), scarlet fever, varicella, clinical appearance, complications
pediatric-exanthems.core: Fever with a childhood rash: use fever timing, rash progression, mucosal findings, immunization status, and pregnancy exposure to distinguish causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incomplete immunization, daycare/school exposure, travel; immunosuppression increases severe viral disease
Pregnant contacts require prompt assessment after rubella, parvovirus, or varicella exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Toxic appearance**, petechiae/purpura, hypotension, meningismus → evaluate invasive infection immediately
Measles: cough, coryza, conjunctivitis precede rash; rubella: posterior auricular/suboccipital adenopathy
Varicella: trunk/scalp predominance; oral mucosal lesions may accompany the skin eruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Parvovirus suppresses erythroid precursors; congenital infection can cause severe fetal anemia
VZV remains latent in sensory ganglia; HHV-6 commonly causes febrile illness in infants

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected measles → **airborne isolation**, notify public health; respiratory PCR plus serum IgM
Scarlet fever → rapid GAS test; negative pediatric test → throat culture
Typical roseola/fifth disease: clinical; atypical vesicles → VZV PCR; rubella → public-health serology/PCR

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scarlet fever → **penicillin or amoxicillin**; other uncomplicated exanthems generally supportive
Measles → hydration, complication care, clinician-supervised vitamin A for children
Severe/immunocompromised varicella → **IV acyclovir**; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Measles: pneumonia, encephalitis, delayed SSPE; rubella: congenital cataracts, deafness, PDA
Parvovirus: aplastic crisis, hydrops, adult symmetric polyarthritis → NSAIDs, not steroids; roseola: febrile seizures
Varicella: bacterial superinfection, pneumonia, cerebellitis; GAS: rheumatic fever, glomerulonephritis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MMR and varicella vaccines**; live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
Measles exposure: MMR within 72 hours or immune globulin within 6 days for eligible contacts

rows.label: Mimics
items: Kawasaki disease: ≥5 days fever, conjunctivitis, oral/extremity changes
Drug eruption: medication exposure without characteristic infectious sequence

table.title: Signature rash
rows: Koplik spots; face → downward confluent rash
Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines, strawberry tongue

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent, traumatic, malignant, or recurrent effusion → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure
Early post-cardiac-surgery tamponade → **urgent mediastinal re-exploration**

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings
Abrupt onset + AF, even with prior claudication → **embolus**, not in situ thrombosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle
Subclavian stenosis proximal to vertebral origin → arm exercise reverses ipsilateral vertebral flow; brachiocephalic lesion: right arm + carotid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; acute ischemia: bedside Doppler, **arteriography with runoff**
Subclavian steal → **compare BP in both arms** (gap >15 mm Hg); confirm with duplex or **MR angiography**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia with distal target → **surgical bypass** before amputation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin, vascular consultation** without awaiting imaging; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible or nonfunctional limb (nonambulatory, contractures) → primary amputation
Popliteal aneurysm: pulsatile popliteal mass, distal emboli; large → **tibial nerve compression** (posterior knee/calf pain)

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings
Thoracic outlet syndrome: symptoms on arm abduction, no posterior-circulation ischemia

table.title: Clinical patterns
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals
Calf claudication; normal femoral, weak pedal pulses
Arm-exercise dizziness/syncope or claudication; weak ipsilateral pulse

personality-disorders.name: Personality disorders
personality-disorders.scope: Cluster A (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal), Cluster B (borderline, antisocial, histrionic, narcissistic), Cluster C (avoidant, dependent, OCPD), dialectical behavior therapy
personality-disorders.core: Enduring, inflexible patterns of cognition, affect, relationships, or impulse control cause impairment across settings beginning by adolescence or early adulthood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Temperament, genetic susceptibility, early adversity and disrupted attachment; avoid attributing diagnosis to trauma alone
Traits must exceed cultural expectations; diagnose cautiously during acute illness or developmental transitions

rows.label: Clues
items: Cluster A: paranoid—distrust; schizoid—detachment; schizotypal—magical thinking, odd speech/perceptions, social discomfort
Cluster B: antisocial—violations of rights; histrionic—attention seeking; narcissistic—grandiosity/entitlement
Cluster C: avoidant—fears rejection/embarrassment, avoids new activities; dependent—clinging; OCPD—rigid perfectionism, control
★ Borderline: **splitting, unstable identity/relationships, self-harm**, abandonment fear, chronic emptiness, impulsivity

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Maladaptive trait patterns impair emotion regulation and interpersonal functioning; no diagnostic biomarker
Impulsive aggression, violent suicide → **low CSF 5-HIAA** (serotonin metabolite)

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Longitudinal clinical assessment** across contexts; obtain collateral with consent
Exclude mood episodes, psychotic illness, substances, neurodevelopmental disorders and acquired brain disease
★ Antisocial diagnosis requires **age ≥18 plus conduct disorder before 15**
Borderline may cause brief stress-related paranoia/dissociation; sustained psychosis requires broader evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Borderline → **dialectical behavior therapy**; structured psychotherapy and consistent team boundaries
Trait-matched psychotherapy, e.g., avoidant → **CBT**, assertiveness training; clear expectations, empathic, nonpunitive tone
No medication treats personality disorder globally; target comorbid depression/anxiety or limited severe symptoms
Self-harm threats → assess intent, plan, access and safety; imminent risk → emergency psychiatric care
Avoid staff splitting through shared care plans; avoid reflexive long-term benzodiazepines in impulsive patients

rows.label: Complications
items: Self-injury/suicide, substance misuse, impaired work/relationships; antisocial traits → legal or violence consequences
Stigma and inconsistent treatment worsen engagement; therapeutic ruptures require careful repair

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autism: early developmental social-communication differences and restricted interests
Delusional disorder: fixed delusion rather than generalized suspicious personality style

personality-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Common diagnostic confusions
rows: Reactive hours-long shifts vs sustained mood episodes
Odd beliefs vs persistent frank psychosis

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure
**Comprehensive, contextual care**: whole-person, longitudinal; tailored to culture, family, goals

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

table.title: Difficult conversations
rows: Pause; allow feelings; schedule prompt follow-up
Voice openly in patient's presence; no covert action
Capable patient hides news from family
Encourage support; respect privacy; never lie to family
Child asks prognosis, parents forbid disclosure
Explore understanding; encourage talking with parents; never lie
Negotiate adherence contract; punitive control backfires
Fluent bilingual staff acceptable; never a child

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

pleural-effusion.name: Pleural effusion
pleural-effusion.scope: Transudate vs exudate (Light criteria), parapneumonic effusion, empyema, malignant effusion
pleural-effusion.core: Fluid in the pleural space causes dyspnea, dullness, and reduced breath sounds; classify by mechanism and identify infection requiring drainage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome; pneumonia, malignancy, pulmonary embolism, TB
Recent thoracic surgery, pancreatitis, esophageal rupture, autoimmune disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Pleuritic pain, reduced fremitus; large effusion shifts mediastinum away; unilateral + cancer history → malignant
Fever or persistent sepsis despite antibiotics suggests complicated parapneumonic fluid/empyema
Bloody fluid: malignancy (prior cancer, mediastinal mass), embolism, trauma; milky → chyle
Foul-smelling pus after aspiration → **anaerobic empyema**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transudate: altered hydrostatic/oncotic pressure; exudate: increased permeability or impaired lymphatic drainage
Heart-failure transudate: pleural protein <3 g/dL, low LDH and cell count; **glucose equals serum**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Chest radiograph → **ultrasound-guided thoracentesis** for new unexplained, unilateral, or atypical effusion
Classic bilateral heart-failure effusions → diuresis first; sample if fever, asymmetry, or treatment failure
★ **Exudate if any Light criterion** positive; compare paired pleural and serum measurements
Pleural pH, glucose, cell differential, Gram stain/culture; cytology if cancer suspected
Diuresis can create pseudoexudate; serum–pleural albumin gradient >1.2 g/dL supports transudate

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat systemic cause; therapeutic thoracentesis for significant symptoms; avoid rapid excessive drainage
★ Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, **pH <7.20** or glucose <60 → empyema/complicated: chest tube, antibiotics
Loculated infected fluid → intrapleural tPA/DNase; persistent sepsis → VATS evaluation
★ Recurrent symptomatic malignancy → **indwelling pleural catheter** or pleurodesis; trapped lung favors catheter

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, loculation, trapped lung, respiratory compromise
Thoracentesis → pneumothorax, bleeding, reexpansion pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Heart-failure control, prompt pneumonia treatment; ultrasound guidance reduces procedural injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atelectasis: mediastinal shift toward volume loss
Consolidation: increased fremitus, bronchial breath sounds
Pneumothorax: hyperresonance rather than dullness

pleural-effusion.evidence: Not checked online; established pleural disease teaching.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.scope: Community-acquired, hospital-acquired, ventilator-associated, aspiration, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma)
pneumonia.core: Acute lower respiratory infection with a new infiltrate; severity, acquisition setting, and resistance risks determine disposition and empiric antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, COPD, age, immunosuppression
Dysphagia, absent gag/cough (stroke, dementia, Parkinson), impaired consciousness → aspiration
HAP ≥48 hours hospitalized; VAP ≥48 hours after intubation
Prior MRSA/Pseudomonas isolation or recent hospitalization with IV antibiotics → resistant pathogens

rows.label: Clues
items: Fever, cough, sputum, focal crackles; older adults: confusion; children: lower-lobe disease may refer abdominal pain
★ Severe: **hypoxemia, hypotension, tachypnea**, multilobar disease; ventilation or pressors → ICU
Legionella: water exposure, diarrhea, hyponatremia; Mycoplasma: school-age/young adult, indolent dry cough, cold agglutinins
Immunocompromised, diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia → **Pneumocystis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alveolar inflammation/exudate → shunt and impaired oxygenation
Chemical aspiration pneumonitis: sterile gastric injury; severity tracks **volume and acidity**; rapid improvement possible

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CXR** first; CT if strong suspicion despite nondiagnostic radiograph
**CURB-65** 0–1 or low PSI → outpatient; severe CAP → blood/sputum cultures, Legionella antigen ± PCR
Low procalcitonin alone does not justify withholding initial antibiotics in radiographically confirmed bacterial CAP
Gram-positive lancet diplococci → **S pneumoniae**: commonest CAP; lobar consolidation, high fever, often post-viral URI
Small gram-negative coccobacilli, smoker/COPD → **H influenzae**

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen, fluids for hypoperfusion; drain empyema; narrow antibiotics to cultures
★ Aspiration pneumonia: usual CAP coverage; **add anaerobic coverage only for abscess/empyema**
Anaerobes: **ampicillin-sulbactam**; older exam questions may expect **clindamycin**, even without abscess
Stable nonsevere CAP: ATS 2025 permits 3–4 days; classic ≥5-day rule remains for severe disease
★ Severe noninfluenza CAP → consider **systemic corticosteroids**; nonsevere CAP → avoid routine steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Parapneumonic effusion, empyema, bacteremia, respiratory failure, sepsis
S aureus: postinfluenza necrotizing pneumonia; child failing amoxicillin, dense consolidation/effusion
Aspiration (alcoholism, intubation) → **lung abscess**: dependent-segment cavity, air-fluid level, foul sputum
Antibiotic exposure → C difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Influenza/pneumococcal vaccination, smoking cessation, swallowing evaluation
Aspiration/VAP prevention: head elevation 30–45°, oral care, early liberation from ventilation

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: thrombotic risk, pleuritic pain, no infectious source
HF: bilateral edema, elevated JVP, cardiac dysfunction

table.title: Empiric adult regimens
rows: Amoxicillin/clavulanate + azithromycin; doxycycline alternative; or levofloxacin
Antipseudomonal: cefepime, ceftazidime, or piperacillin/tazobactam; usually 7 days

pneumothorax.name: Pneumothorax
