pneumothorax.scope: Spontaneous pneumothorax (primary, secondary), tension pneumothorax, needle decompression, chest tube thoracostomy
pneumothorax.core: Pleural air causes acute unilateral pleuritic pain and reduced breath sounds; circulatory compromise indicates tension physiology requiring immediate decompression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Primary: tall thin young adults, smoking, family history
Secondary: COPD, cystic fibrosis, PJP, interstitial lung disease; trauma/procedures or positive-pressure ventilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral hyperresonance, dyspnea, asymmetric chest expansion; severity depends on underlying reserve
★ **Hypotension + distended neck veins + unilateral absent breath sounds** → tension; tracheal deviation is late
Ventilated: positive pressure converts occult pneumothorax to tension; sudden desaturation, rising airway pressure, collapse

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of negative pleural pressure permits lung collapse
One-way air entry increases intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and causing obstructive shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable tension suspicion → **clinical diagnosis; no imaging delay**
Stable → upright chest radiograph: visceral pleural line with absent peripheral markings
Bedside ultrasound: absent sliding/B-lines supports; lung point highly specific; absent sliding alone nonspecific
CT for uncertain/complex cases; supine radiograph may show deep sulcus rather than apical air

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension → **immediate needle or finger thoracostomy**, then chest tube; oxygen and resuscitation
Needle commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space anterior/midaxillary, or second midclavicular; insert above rib
★ Minimal symptoms, stable: primary (any size) or small iatrogenic → **observation**, reliable follow-up
Symptomatic/large primary → aspiration or small-bore chest tube; secondary generally admit, drain if symptomatic/significant
Persistent air leak, recurrence, bilateral disease, or high-risk occupation → VATS bleb treatment/pleurodesis

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, tension progression, recurrence; reexpansion pulmonary edema after drainage
Chest tube → bleeding, infection, organ injury; blocked/clamped drain may recreate tension

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Smoking cessation**; avoid flying until radiographic resolution and clearance
Scuba diving contraindicated without specialist assessment/definitive prevention; counsel recurrence warning symptoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: PE: pleuritic pain with preserved lung sliding, embolic risk
Giant bulla: intraparenchymal thin wall; CT if stable uncertainty before tube
Tamponade: shock with pericardial fluid rather than unilateral absent ventilation
Massive hemothorax: dullness, collapsed neck veins rather than distended

pneumothorax.evidence: Conservative care checked 2026-10-30: [BTS pleural guideline 2023](https://doi.org/10.1136/thorax-2022-219784); tension rescue: established emergency teaching.

polycystic-ovary-syndrome.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.scope: Rotterdam criteria (hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovaries), metabolic risks, weight loss, oral contraceptives, ovulation induction (letrozole, clomiphene)
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.core: Hyperandrogenism and chronic ovulatory dysfunction after exclusion of alternative causes suggest PCOS; management follows metabolic, menstrual and fertility priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, insulin resistance and obesity; lean patients can also have PCOS
Pubertal transition can mimic disease, requiring stricter adolescent diagnostic criteria

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular/infrequent menses, episodic heavy bleeding, infertility, hirsutism, acne or androgenic alopecia
Acanthosis nigricans suggests hyperinsulinemia; obesity is supportive, not required
Rapid virilization, deep voice or markedly elevated androgens → investigate tumor rather than assume PCOS

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insulin resistance and ovarian androgen excess impair follicular maturation and ovulation
Absent cyclic progesterone permits persistent estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adults: **2 of 3 Rotterdam** features—hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, polycystic ovarian morphology
Exclude mimics: **hCG, TSH, prolactin, morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone**; latter screens nonclassic CAH
Total/free testosterone; **clinical hirsutism/acne** suffices despite normal levels; DHEAS if adrenal source suspected
★ Irregular cycles plus hyperandrogenism → **ultrasound not required**; LH:FSH ratio not diagnostic
BP, lipid profile and **oral glucose tolerance test** assess metabolic risk; adolescent diagnosis avoids ultrasound criteria

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Lifestyle/weight management first for all; modest weight loss can restore ovulation in overweight patients
★ No pregnancy desired → **combined OCP** for cycles/androgen symptoms; cyclic progestin or LNG-IUD protects endometrium
Persistent hirsutism → spironolactone with reliable contraception; allow months for hair response
Metabolic risk/insulin resistance → metformin; less effective than OCP for androgen symptoms
★ Anovulatory infertility → **letrozole first-line**; clomiphene alternative, older exams may expect it; check other factors

rows.label: Complications
items: Endometrial hyperplasia/cancer, infertility, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, OSA and depression
Pregnancy → increased gestational diabetes and hypertensive-disorder risk
Gonadotropin ovulation induction → high multiple-gestation risk, so letrozole/clomiphene first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for prolonged amenorrhea; persistent abnormal bleeding → endometrial assessment
Periodic glycemic/BP/lipid reassessment; preconception metabolic optimization and folate

rows.label: Mimics
items: Androgen-secreting tumor: rapid progression, severe virilization
Nonclassic CAH: elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone
Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: low estrogen with exercise/energy deficit

potassium-disorders.name: Potassium disorders
potassium-disorders.scope: Hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, cardiac membrane stabilization, shift therapy, elimination
potassium-disorders.core: Potassium abnormalities can cause weakness and fatal arrhythmias; stabilize cardiac risk while identifying the cause and correcting total-body balance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hyperkalemia: AKI/CKD, RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue lysis, insulin deficiency
Hypokalemia: GI losses, loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, insulin/beta-agonists, magnesium depletion

rows.label: Clues
items: Flaccid weakness, paralysis, palpitations; symptoms may be absent despite dangerous levels
★ **K ≥6.5 mmol/L, ECG changes, or rapid rise** → emergency; normal ECG not reassuring
Bradycardia/high-degree AV block with renal failure → suspect hyperkalemia; calcium before pacemaker

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extracellular K changes alter membrane excitability and cardiac conduction
Acidosis/insulin deficiency shift K outward; intracellular shifts can coexist with severe total-body depletion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG + repeat potassium**, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, magnesium; assess drugs and acid-base status
Hemolysis, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis → pseudohyperkalemia; repeat atraumatic draw if clinically compatible
Hypokalemia: urine K distinguishes renal wasting from extrarenal loss; interpret with BP/acid-base pattern
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory blood draw when malignant ECG changes present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hyperkalemic ECG changes or dialysis-patient arrest → **IV calcium gluconate/chloride first**; protects myocardium only
★ Shift K inward: **IV insulin + dextrose**, nebulized albuterol; bicarbonate mainly with significant acidosis
Remove K: loop diuretic if urine output, selected binders; urgent dialysis for severe refractory/renal-failure cases
Mild/stable hypokalemia → oral KCl; <2.5, arrhythmia, paralysis, or no oral access → monitored IV replacement
★ **Correct magnesium deficiency** for refractory low K; never give IV potassium push; monitor glucose after insulin

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, respiratory muscle failure
Overcorrection, rebound dyskalemia; insulin-induced hypoglycemia; IV potassium extravasation/phlebitis
Diuretic hypokalemia → **digoxin toxicity**, multifocal PVCs; check K first

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review supplements/salt substitutes; monitor K/creatinine after diuretic or RAAS-drug changes
Treat diarrhea/vomiting and underlying mineralocorticoid disorders; replace ongoing losses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexic weakness without explanatory electrolyte pattern
Periodic paralysis: episodic shifts, sometimes thyrotoxicosis; avoid excessive replacement causing rebound

table.title: ECG patterns
rows: Peaked T → PR prolongation → wide QRS/sine-wave
Flat T, ST depression, prominent U waves

potassium-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established electrolyte emergency principles.

pressure-injuries.name: Pressure injuries
pressure-injuries.scope: Stage 1 through 4 pressure injuries, unstageable eschar, risk assessment (Braden scale), pressure offloading, repositioning, wound debridement, dressing selection
pressure-injuries.core: Sustained pressure and shear damage skin and deeper tissue over bony prominences or beneath medical devices.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Immobility, spinal cord injury, impaired sensation, poor perfusion, malnutrition
Moisture/incontinence, friction, advanced age; oxygen tubing and immobilization devices create focal loading

rows.label: Clues
items: Sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, occiput and device contact sites; pain may precede visible injury
Dark skin: assess temperature, induration and discoloration rather than redness alone
Purulence, spreading erythema, fever or worsening pain → infection; exposed bone raises osteomyelitis concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Capillary compression and tissue deformation → ischemia/reperfusion damage; shear increases deep injury
Surface appearance may underestimate muscle injury; stages describe depth, not a required progression

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspect skin and document depth**, drainage, undermining and surrounding tissue
Braden scale assesses sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition and friction/shear
Suspected osteomyelitis → MRI and, when feasible, bone biopsy/culture; superficial swabs poorly specific
Healing lesions retain their original highest stage; **never reverse-stage**

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Offload pressure**, support surfaces and individualized repositioning; float heels with pillows under calves
Saline cleansing; shallow/low-exudate → hydrocolloid; draining → foam/alginate; maintain moisture, protect surrounding skin
★ Necrotic tissue → debridement, except **stable dry heel/ischemic eschar** without infection
Systemic antibiotics only for cellulitis, sepsis or osteomyelitis; not colonization alone
Deep defects → **oral protein/calorie supplements** if malnourished, not parenteral; then negative-pressure, flap closure

rows.label: Complications
items: Cellulitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis, chronic pain and functional decline

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily skin checks, mobilization, moisture barriers and adequate protein/calories
Avoid donut cushions, massage over prominences; reassess device fit and risk whenever clinical status changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Incontinence dermatitis: diffuse superficial moisture-associated damage, not focal loading
Arterial ulcer: distal ischemic site, weak pulses

table.title: Stage by visible depth
rows: Partial thickness; exposed dermis or serum blister
Full thickness; fat visible; no deep structures
Exposed/palpable fascia, muscle, tendon or bone
Persistent maroon/purple discoloration or blood blister

preterm-labor.name: Preterm labor
preterm-labor.scope: Preterm labor (<37 weeks), cervical insufficiency, tocolysis (indomethacin, nifedipine), antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone), magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection, GBS chemoprophylaxis
preterm-labor.core: Regular contractions with cervical change before 37 weeks; briefly delay eligible early births to improve neonatal outcomes, without prolonging unsafe pregnancies.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior spontaneous preterm birth, short cervix, multiple gestation, infection, smoking, uterine anomalies
Cervical surgery or prior painless second-trimester loss suggests cervical insufficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Pelvic pressure, backache, increased discharge, contractions; assess membrane rupture and bleeding
Fever, uterine tenderness, fetal tachycardia → intraamniotic infection; maternal/fetal instability changes delivery timing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Premature inflammatory/uterine activation versus mechanically weak cervix with painless dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Sterile speculum examination** for pooling and cervix; ultrasound dates pregnancy and assesses presentation
Transvaginal cervical length; selected symptomatic cases: negative fetal fibronectin predicts low imminent birth risk
Collect GBS culture, urine studies; exclude previa before digital examination with bleeding

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Birth within 7 days, **24–33 6/7 weeks** → betamethasone; selected untreated 34–36 6/7-week pregnancies also eligible
★ Delivery expected <32 weeks → **magnesium sulfate** for neuroprotection, not primary tocolysis
Tocolysis: 48 hours for steroids/transfer; no maintenance; late-preterm steroids avoided with pregestational diabetes
★ **No tocolysis** with infection, significant abruption, severe preeclampsia, or fetal compromise; proceed toward delivery
Intrapartum penicillin for positive/unknown GBS; no routine antibiotics for intact membranes without infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Neonatal RDS, IVH, NEC, sepsis, cerebral palsy; magnesium toxicity → hyporeflexia, respiratory depression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Singleton short cervix ≤20 mm before 24 weeks → vaginal progesterone; consider at 21–25 mm
Cervical insufficiency/prior qualifying loss → cerclage; prior preterm birth + cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks
17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate withdrawn 2023; progesterone without short cervix not routinely recommended
Older exam questions may expect 17-hydroxyprogesterone from 16–20 weeks after prior spontaneous preterm birth

rows.label: Mimics
items: Braxton Hicks: no progressive dilation
Cervical insufficiency: painless dilation, minimal contractions
PPROM: membrane rupture precedes labor; distinct latency-antibiotic pathway

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular/CGRP signaling; aura: cortical spreading depolarization, visual → contralateral occipital lobe
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent migraine → propranolol, topiramate, CGRP drugs; pregnancy → **acetaminophen**; no ergots, topiramate, valproate
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura
Triptan + **ergotamine within 24 hours** → additive vasoconstriction: prolonged vasospasm, MI, stroke

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers
Migraine escalation after starting estrogen, normal exam → **stop estrogen** before imaging or added analgesics

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
psoriasis.scope: Plaque psoriasis, nail pitting and onycholysis, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon, psoriatic arthritis, topical and systemic therapy
psoriasis.core: Sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, usually on extensor surfaces or scalp; inspect nails and screen for inflammatory arthritis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, obesity, smoking, alcohol; stress, trauma, streptococcal infection
Lithium, beta blockers, antimalarials; systemic glucocorticoid withdrawal can trigger severe rebound

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Nail pitting, onycholysis**, oil-drop discoloration support diagnosis
Auspitz sign: pinpoint bleeding after scale removal; Koebner phenomenon: lesions at trauma sites
Psoriatic arthritis: morning stiffness, DIP disease, dactylitis, enthesitis, asymmetric or axial involvement
Generalized pustules, erythroderma, fever, hemodynamic disturbance → urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated TNF/IL-23/Th17 activation → accelerated keratinocyte turnover

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; biopsy if atypical; assess body surface area and functional impact
KOH scraping if fungal infection possible; inflammatory joint symptoms warrant rheumatology assessment
Before biologics: TB, hepatitis screening; before methotrexate: CBC, liver and renal tests, pregnancy assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized plaques → **topical corticosteroid + calcipotriene**; choose potency by site
Face/folds: low-potency steroid briefly or tacrolimus; emollients and scale removal aid penetration
★ Extensive/refractory disease → **narrowband UVB**, methotrexate, or targeted biologic; arthritis requires systemic control
Methotrexate contraindicated in pregnancy and significant liver disease; cyclosporine useful for rapid short-term control
Avoid routine systemic steroids; unstable erythrodermic/pustular disease → hospital support and specialist treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Joint destruction, depression, cardiometabolic disease; severe skin failure → fluid loss and infection
Systemic immunosuppression → infections; methotrexate → hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, weight management, limit alcohol; screen BP, lipids, diabetes, depression; reduce skin trauma

rows.label: Mimics
items: Tinea corporis: annular advancing edge, positive KOH
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale in sebaceous areas
Atopic dermatitis: flexural eczema with marked pruritus

psoriasis.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatology and psoriatic arthritis teaching.

pulmonary-hypertension.name: Pulmonary hypertension
pulmonary-hypertension.scope: WHO groups 1-5 (PAH, left heart disease, lung disease/hypoxia, CTEPH, multifactorial), cor pulmonale, echocardiography, right heart catheterization, endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors
pulmonary-hypertension.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart failure with elevated pulmonary pressures requires hemodynamic classification before vasodilator treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Connective-tissue disease, congenital shunts, portal hypertension, HIV, methamphetamine → PAH
Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia or prior pulmonary embolism are common secondary contexts

rows.label: Clues
items: Loud P2, RV heave, tricuspid regurgitation murmur; exertional chest pain or presyncope
JVD, hepatomegaly and edema → right-heart failure/cor pulmonale
Severe dyspnea with relatively preserved spirometry or low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary vascular resistance or elevated left filling pressure increases RV afterload
Sustained pressure overload → RV hypertrophy, dilation, reduced output and systemic venous congestion
Chronic alveolar hypoxia (COPD, OSA) → **pulmonary vasoconstriction** and remodeling → raised vascular resistance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography** estimates probability and evaluates RV/left-heart function; not definitive pressure diagnosis
★ **Right-heart catheterization: mean PAP >20 mm Hg** at rest confirms PH
Precapillary: wedge ≤15 mm Hg and **PVR >2 Wood units**; postcapillary: wedge >15
★ **V/Q scan** screens CTEPH; normal perfusion essentially excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
PFT/DLCO, chest CT, sleep evaluation, HIV/autoimmune testing by history; vasoreactivity testing in selected PAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen for hypoxemia, diuresis for congestion; treat underlying disease and refer confirmed PAH/CTEPH
★ PAH → specialist **endothelin antagonist + PDE-5 inhibitor**; high-risk disease → parenteral prostacyclin
Vasoreactive idiopathic/heritable/drug-associated PAH → selected high-dose calcium-channel blocker; not empiric treatment
CTEPH → lifelong anticoagulation and pulmonary endarterectomy if operable; selected balloon angioplasty or riociguat
Do not routinely use PAH vasodilators for left-heart/lung-disease PH; PDE-5 drugs cannot combine with nitrates/riociguat

rows.label: Complications
items: RV failure, arrhythmia, syncope and death; pregnancy carries substantial maternal risk in PAH
Endothelin antagonists are teratogenic; some require liver monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid methamphetamine, address thromboembolic risk; vaccination, supervised exercise, pregnancy/contraception counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: HFpEF: elevated wedge pressure identifies postcapillary cause
Deconditioning/anemia: no catheter-confirmed pulmonary pressure elevation

raynaud-phenomenon.name: Raynaud phenomenon
raynaud-phenomenon.core: Episodic cold- or stress-triggered digital vasospasm produces reversible color changes; asymmetric painful attacks or tissue injury suggest secondary disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young women, family history; smoking, vibration tools, cold exposure
Systemic sclerosis, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease; stimulants, beta blockers, ergot derivatives

rows.label: Clues
items: Pallor → cyanosis → reactive redness; numbness or tingling; all three phases not required
★ Digital **ulcers, pitting scars, gangrene** require evaluation for secondary vasculopathy
Sclerodactyly, telangiectasia, reflux, inflammatory arthritis, rash, or dyspnea → connective tissue disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Exaggerated arteriolar smooth-muscle constriction; secondary disease adds endothelial injury and structural vasculopathy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical history + nailfold capillaroscopy**; inspect pulses and both hands
Suspected secondary disease → ANA, ESR/CRP, CBC, urinalysis; disease-specific antibodies based on findings
Suspected proximal/occlusive disease → arterial Doppler and vascular consultation
Normal inflammatory tests do not override tissue-threatening clinical findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Warm core and hands, stop nicotine and vasoconstricting drugs; **dihydropyridine CCB** for persistent symptoms
Nifedipine or amlodipine first-line; monitor headache, edema, hypotension
CCB-refractory or CCB-intolerant → sildenafil or topical nitrate; do not combine PDE-5 inhibitor with nitrates
★ Critical ischemia → urgent admission, **IV prostacyclin**, vascular/rheumatology consultation; treat underlying disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary disease → infection, ulceration, infarction, tissue loss
Primary disease rarely causes permanent damage; evolving systemic findings warrant reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Layered clothing, gloves, avoid rapid temperature changes; stress management and vibration-exposure reduction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acrocyanosis: persistent painless blue hands, no discrete attacks
Erythromelalgia: burning red extremities worsened by heat
Peripheral arterial disease: persistent ischemia with diminished pulses

raynaud-phenomenon.evidence: Not checked online; established rheumatology teaching.

rhabdomyolysis.name: Rhabdomyolysis
rhabdomyolysis.scope: Trauma, crush injury, prolonged immobilization, statins, seizures, elevated CK, myoglobinuria (blood on dipstick without RBCs), acute tubular necrosis, aggressive IV saline hydration
rhabdomyolysis.core: Acute skeletal muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and electrolytes; recognize pigment nephropathy early and restore renal perfusion before kidney failure develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Crush injury, prolonged immobilization**, compartment syndrome, ischemia/reperfusion
Seizures, strenuous exercise, heatstroke, cocaine; statins, especially with interacting drugs
Hypokalemia, infections, alcohol intoxication; pressure injury during unconsciousness

rows.label: Clues
items: Muscle pain, weakness, swelling; dark urine possible, but classic triad often incomplete
↑K, ↑phosphate, early ↓Ca; AST may rise from muscle rather than liver
Tense painful compartment, pain with passive stretch, sensory change → concurrent limb emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Myocyte necrosis → pigment-mediated tubular injury and casts, amplified by hypovolemia and aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK >5 times upper limit**, often >1,000 U/L; trend until clearly declining
★ Urine dipstick **heme positive with few/no RBCs** → myoglobin; negative result cannot exclude
Electrolytes, creatinine, ECG, urine output; CK magnitude supports risk assessment, not dialysis alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early **IV normal saline**; titrate to urine output 1–3 mL/kg/hour, avoiding overload
Stop culprit; treat heatstroke/seizures; compartment syndrome → emergency fasciotomy
Hyperkalemic ECG changes → IV calcium, insulin/dextrose; dialysis for refractory electrolyte/volume/acid-base disturbances
★ **No routine bicarbonate or mannitol** for AKI prevention; anuria → reassess fluids, renal consultation
Asymptomatic hypocalcemia → avoid replacement; symptomatic tetany or arrhythmia → calcium

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute tubular necrosis, dangerous arrhythmias, disseminated intravascular coagulation
Recovery phase → rebound hypercalcemia; excessive fluids with renal failure → pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration and gradual exercise progression; avoid exertion during severe heat or illness
Review statin interactions, especially macrolides/gemfibrozil; pressure relief during prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hematuria: numerous RBCs on microscopy
Hemolysis: heme-positive urine with anemia, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin rather than marked CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: subacute proximal weakness without acute toxic/traumatic trigger

rhabdomyolysis.evidence: Fluid targets and bicarbonate guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAST consensus, 2022](https://tsaco.bmj.com/content/7/1/e000836.full.pdf).

secondary-hypertension.name: Secondary hypertension
secondary-hypertension.scope: Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, diagnostic workup
secondary-hypertension.core: Abrupt, unusually young, severe, or resistant hypertension suggests a treatable secondary driver.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Renal stenosis: older smoker → atherosclerotic **lipid plaque**; young/middle-aged woman → **fibromuscular dysplasia** (medial hyperplasia, renal + carotid)
Renal disease, adrenal tumors, sleep apnea
NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, stimulants, glucocorticoids, licorice; medication nonadherence can mimic resistance

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis** → aldosterone excess, primary or renovascular; normal K does not exclude it
**Abdominal bruit**, diffuse atherosclerosis, late abrupt worsening, small unilateral kidney → renal artery stenosis
Flash pulmonary edema or creatinine rise >30% after ACE inhibitor/ARB → renovascular disease
**Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations** → pheochromocytoma; cushingoid appearance, upper-body hypertension guide testing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Renal hypoperfusion → juxtaglomerular **renin** → RAAS; ACE inhibitor removes efferent constriction → ↓renal flow, ↓GFR across stenosis
Autonomous aldosterone → distal sodium absorption, potassium loss, low renin; pressure natriuresis escape prevents edema
Adrenal medullary catecholamine or cortisol excess, aortic obstruction, or nocturnal hypoxia increases vascular pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **home/ambulatory BP**, adherence, cuff technique; BMP, urinalysis, creatinine, TSH
Sleep-apnea symptoms → polysomnography; abnormal urinary sediment → renal ultrasound and kidney evaluation
★ Biochemical testing precedes adrenal imaging; correct hypokalemia and account for interfering medications
Endocrine Society 2025: suggest **aldosterone screening for all hypertension**, conditional on resources

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Primary aldosteronism: unilateral → **adrenalectomy**; bilateral → spironolactone/eplerenone
Renovascular atherosclerosis → medical risk reduction; revascularize selected recurrent pulmonary edema or refractory disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia → angioplasty; critical bilateral renal stenosis → avoid ACE inhibitor/ARB
★ Pheochromocytoma: **alpha blockade before beta blockade**, volume expansion, then surgery
Treat cortisol source, repair significant coarctation, use CPAP for OSA; stop contributing drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can cause catecholamine crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor renal function/K after RAAS blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists
Genetic evaluation/family screening for suspected hereditary pheochromocytoma or congenital aortic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: normal out-of-office readings
Essential hypertension: gradual course without specific endocrine/renal clues

table.title: Targeted workup
rows: Selective suppression test; CT/adrenal venous sampling
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines

secondary-hypertension.evidence: Aldosterone screening checked 2026-10-30: [Endocrine Society 2025](https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2); other causes: established teaching.

septic-arthritis.name: Septic arthritis
septic-arthritis.scope: Nongonococcal, gonococcal, prosthetic joint infection, IV drug use, empiric coverage (vancomycin + cefepime), contiguous osteomyelitis
septic-arthritis.core: Acutely painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion → urgent aspiration and drainage; delayed treatment rapidly destroys cartilage.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prosthesis, recent surgery/injection, rheumatoid arthritis, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteremia
IV drug use → S aureus and gram-negative risk, including Pseudomonas
Young sexually active adults → disseminated gonorrhea; adjacent ulcers/osteomyelitis → contiguous spread
RA joint with new febrile monoarthritis → infection until aspirated, not flare

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually acute monoarthritis, often knee; fever may be absent, especially in older/immunocompromised adults
★ **Severe pain with both active and passive motion**; inability to bear weight; child's hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated
Gonococcal dissemination: migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis, sparse pustules; may progress to purulent monoarthritis
Prosthetic infection: persistent pain, loosening, wound drainage or sinus tract, sometimes minimal systemic illness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation → neutrophilic enzymes damage articular cartilage
Implant biofilm limits antibiotic eradication without surgical source control
★ **S aureus** most common, including RA-damaged joints: gram-positive cocci in clusters
Asplenia or recent pharyngitis → **streptococci**: gram-positive cocci in chains

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Arthrocentesis before antibiotics** when stable: cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Synovial WBC >50,000/µL, neutrophil predominance supports infection; lower counts or negative Gram stain never exclude
★ **Crystals do not exclude infection**; send cultures even when gout seems likely
Blood cultures; gonococcal: aspirate on **chocolate/Thayer-Martin agar** plus mucosal NAAT; MRI for suspected contiguous osteomyelitis
New warmth/effusion in OA joint → aspirate before any intra-articular steroid

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ After cultures → **IV vancomycin + cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam** for severe disease, IV drug use, gram-negative risk
Stable low-risk adult: vancomycin ± ceftriaxone based on exposure; narrow to organism/susceptibility
Sepsis → immediate antibiotics without delaying for aspiration; large joints: arthroscopic washout; **hip → operative drainage**, not serial aspiration
Persistent symptoms → repeat drainage, seek abscess/osteomyelitis; mobilize after infection controlled

rows.label: Complications
items: Irreversible joint destruction, avascular necrosis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia, sepsis
Prolonged antibiotics → renal injury, line complications, C difficile; prolonged immobility → stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Sterile procedures, treat skin infections, injection-harm reduction
Gonorrhea: treat partners, screen other STIs, abstain until treatment completed and partners treated

rows.label: Mimics
items: Crystal arthritis: polarized crystals; infection still possible concurrently
Bursitis: localized periarticular swelling, passive joint motion relatively preserved
Reactive arthritis: sterile inflammatory arthritis after GI/GU infection
Transient synovitis (child): afebrile, bears weight, ESR <40, WBC <12,000

table.title: Special treatment branches
rows: Debridement, implant retention, prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk
Procedure bleeding: thoracentesis → intercostal artery, hemothorax; splenectomy → hemoperitoneum, left shoulder pain

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: **lost sympathetic tone** → hypotension, bradycardia or no tachycardia, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid
Warm sepsis: high output, **high mixed venous O2**; pump failure: low contractility, congestion; hypovolemia: low preload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
**Serial lactate**: hypoperfusion, best predicts course and mortality; trend with capillary refill, urine output
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation
CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, IV access; **isotonic crystalloid** (balanced, 0.9% saline) before imaging; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + blood products** (emergency O-negative); crystalloid as bridge; no vasopressors
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone
Pulmonary edema after fluids → stop boluses, **inotrope**; children: epinephrine preferred, older exams may expect dopamine

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose
Isolated head injury: hypertension + bradycardia (Cushing); trauma hypotension + tachycardia → assume hemorrhage

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

sickle-cell-disease.name: Sickle cell disease
sickle-cell-disease.scope: Vaso-occlusive pain crisis, acute chest syndrome, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis, stroke, sickle cell trait, hemoglobin electrophoresis
sickle-cell-disease.core: HbS polymerization causes chronic hemolysis and episodic vascular occlusion; fever, hypoxemia and focal neurologic deficits require urgent escalation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autosomal recessive β-globin disease; dehydration, hypoxemia, cold and infection trigger sickling
Functional asplenia → encapsulated infection from early childhood; **S. pneumoniae** leads pneumonia and fulminant sepsis

rows.label: Clues
items: Baseline anemia, reticulocytosis, jaundice; childhood dactylitis or recurrent severe bone pain
Acute chest syndrome: **new pulmonary infiltrate** plus fever, respiratory symptoms or hypoxemia
Sequestration: sudden splenomegaly, falling hemoglobin, shock; aplasia: **low reticulocyte count**, often parvovirus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Deoxygenated hemoglobin polymerizes → rigid erythrocytes, endothelial injury, ischemia and shortened RBC survival
Acute chest trigger: **infection** most common; in situ thrombosis and fat embolism less often
Severe anemia → low viscosity, vasodilation, ↓afterload → **↑cardiac output** preserves oxygen delivery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC confirms genotype; newborn screen detects disease before symptoms
Crisis → CBC, reticulocytes, bilirubin; fever → blood cultures; respiratory symptoms → chest radiograph
New focal deficit → emergency brain imaging, without delaying transfusion preparation
Distinguish osteomyelitis from infarction using cultures and MRI when focal fever/pain persists

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pain crisis → prompt **IV opioid**, morphine (AKI: lower dose or hydromorphone); no meperidine; NSAID only if kidneys normal
Pain crisis support: euvolemic hydration; oxygen only for hypoxemia; no routine transfusion
★ Acute chest → oxygen, **ceftriaxone + azithromycin**, incentive spirometry; transfuse for significant anemia
Severe acute chest, stroke → **urgent exchange transfusion**; sequestration (cautious) or aplasia → simple transfusion
Fever → immediate **IV ceftriaxone/cefotaxime**, despite daily penicillin prophylaxis

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, avascular necrosis, priapism, pigment gallstones, nephropathy, retinopathy
Repeated transfusions → alloimmunization and iron overload; delayed hyperhemolysis can worsen anemia
Chronic hemolysis → ↑folate demand → **folate deficiency**, macrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Hydroxyurea** raises HbF, reduces crises; monitor CBC
Penicillin prophylaxis through age 5 in HbSS; pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib and influenza vaccines
Annual transcranial Doppler ages 2–16 in HbSS/HbSβ0; abnormal → chronic transfusion program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomyelitis: persistent localized pain, fever; Salmonella or S. aureus
Iron deficiency: low ferritin, no hemolytic pattern

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics
Functional blindness: intact **pupillary reflex, threat blink, optokinetic nystagmus**
Extreme fever + normal pulse/labs → suspect falsification; **supervised rectal temperature** before antibiotics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic: **incompatible signs**: Hoover, give-way weakness, midline sensory split, forehead vibration discrepancy
Nonepileptic seizures: captured spell without **video-EEG** epileptiform change; often acute stressor
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression
Functional deficits → empathic explanation, expected recovery; nonepileptic seizures → **CBT**, no antiseizure drugs
★ Functional deficit or negative workups → **psychiatric assessment**, no more procedures; **new red flags → reassess**
Factitious: team approach, factual records, no confrontation, evaluate psychiatric comorbidity; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
Factitious disorder imposed on another → serious abuse risk requiring safeguarding action

rows.label: Mimics
items: Occult medical disease: evolving objective findings or coherent physiologic abnormalities
Delusional disorder: fixed somatic belief despite evidence, without flexible doubt

table.title: Distinguishing patterns
rows: Motor/sensory symptoms incompatible with neurologic disease
Intentional deception; no obvious external reward
Intentional symptoms, external gain; no treatment/invasive testing

somatic-symptom-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established DSM-5-TR teaching.

spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression
Anticoagulation + epidural catheter placement/removal → **spinal epidural hematoma**: acute paraplegia, incontinence

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

substance-use-disorders.name: Substance use disorders
substance-use-disorders.scope: Diagnostic criteria (mild, moderate, severe), cocaine use disorder, amphetamine use disorder, cannabis use disorder, motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioral therapy, 12-step programs
substance-use-disorders.core: A problematic pattern causing impaired control, risky use, social impairment or physiologic adaptation defines substance use disorder; severity follows criterion count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, trauma, psychiatric comorbidity, early exposure, unstable housing and peer availability
Persistent psychosocial stress and limited treatment access worsen trajectory

rows.label: Clues
items: Tolerance/withdrawal not required; physiologic adaptation during prescribed use alone does not establish disorder
Stimulant withdrawal: fatigue, hypersomnia, depression and craving; assess suicide risk
Cannabis withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, insomnia and reduced appetite after sustained use
Caffeine withdrawal: diffuse headache 12–48 h after stopping intake, including NPO surgery; normal neurologic exam

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reward learning and neuroadaptation strengthen cue-driven behavior while impairing control
Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake; amphetamines increase release; cannabinoids act mainly at CB1 receptors
THC lipophilic, adipose-stored: urine positive for weeks in chronic use; other drugs clear in days

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **≥2 of 11 DSM-5 criteria in 12 months**; severity **mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6**
Control/social: larger/longer use, failed cutdown, time spent, craving, role failure, social problems, abandoned activities
Risk/pharmacologic: hazardous use, continued despite physical/psychological harm, tolerance, withdrawal
Clinical interview establishes disorder; urine drug testing documents exposure, not severity or current impairment
Screen co-occurring depression, psychosis, HIV/hepatitis risk and polysubstance use; confirm unexpected immunoassay positives

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Motivational interviewing**: explore ambivalence, elicit personal goals, support autonomy; avoid confrontation
★ Stimulant disorder → **contingency management**, CBT/community reinforcement; no FDA-approved maintenance drug
Cannabis disorder → motivational enhancement, CBT and contingency management; no established approved medication
Peer/12-step programs as adjuncts; tailor outpatient versus residential intensity to safety/support and impairment
Stimulant agitation → benzodiazepines/cooling; uncomplicated cannabis intoxication, mild paranoia → observe, no drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Cocaine/amphetamine → MI, stroke, arrhythmia, psychosis; chronic methamphetamine → cardiomyopathy and dental injury
Cannabis → impaired driving, hyperemesis (cessation, fluids, capsaicin/haloperidol), anxiety or psychosis
Stimulant crash can precipitate severe depression/suicidality; withdrawal usually lacks alcohol-like autonomic danger
Older adults: new benzodiazepine (temazepam) → subacute ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, falls

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Harm reduction: **naloxone** for possible opioid contamination, avoid using alone, offer fentanyl testing access
Treat comorbid illness, relapse planning, overdose education and regular follow-up; recurrence prompts reassessment
Adolescent experimentation without impairment → counsel teen and family; no formal treatment program

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bipolar mania: episodes persist independently of intoxication
Primary psychosis: symptoms outside substance exposure periods
ADHD: longstanding childhood-onset pattern, not episodic intoxication

substance-use-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ASAM/AAAP stimulant guideline 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11105801/); DSM-5 criteria established definitions.

table.title: Intoxication by substance
rows: Mydriasis, hypertension, hyperreflexia, paranoia, pressured speech
Violent agitation, hyperthermia; formication with excoriations; MDMA empathic
Red conjunctivae, dry mouth, tachycardia, hunger, slowed time
**Nystagmus**, analgesia, hypertension, myoclonus; violent-catatonic fluctuation, mutism
Perioral/perinasal rash, solvent odor, ataxia/slurring; clears <1 hour
Coma, apnea, hypotension, bradycardia, sluggish pupils

syncope.name: Syncope
syncope.scope: Vasovagal / neurocardiogenic syncope, orthostatic syncope, situational syncope, cardiogenic syncope, breath-holding spells, cerebral hypoperfusion workup
syncope.core: Brief loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid spontaneous recovery; identify cardiac danger before labeling an episode reflex-mediated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Dehydration, blood loss, autonomic dysfunction, diuretics, nitrates, alpha-1 blockers; prolonged standing, heat, fear
Structural heart disease, conduction disease, arrhythmias, family history of sudden death

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Exertional or supine syncope**, palpitations, absent prodrome, cardiac murmur → high-risk cause
Reflex prodrome: nausea, warmth, diaphoresis, tunnel vision; may include brief myoclonic jerks
Situational triggers: urination, coughing, defecation; breath-holding spells follow crying/pain in young children
Shaving, tight collar, head turning + bradycardia → **carotid sinus hypersensitivity**; confirm with carotid sinus massage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Vasodilation/bradycardia, failed postural compensation, or low cardiac output transiently limits cerebral flow

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Initial **history, examination, orthostatic BP, ECG**; bedside glucose and targeted pregnancy/bleeding evaluation
Orthostasis: systolic fall ≥20 or diastolic ≥10 mm Hg within 3 minutes standing
High-risk → admission/monitoring; suspected structural disease → echo; intermittent arrhythmia → ambulatory ECG
Tilt-table testing for recurrent unexplained reflex/orthostatic cases; no routine head CT, EEG, carotid ultrasound
Typical breath-holding spells: normal development, awake trigger, rapid recovery; CBC/ferritin and ECG when evaluating

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Reflex event → supine, legs elevated; **hydration, counterpressure maneuvers**, trigger recognition
Orthostatic cause → replace volume, review drugs, rise slowly, compression; refractory neurogenic cases → midodrine
★ Cardiac cause → **treat rhythm/obstruction**, restrict unsafe activity pending evaluation
Breath-holding: reassure caregivers, safe positioning, treat iron deficiency; no antiseizure drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, fractures, driving injury; underlying cardiac disease carries sudden-death risk
Recurrent episodes → activity limitation, anxiety; pressor drugs can cause supine hypertension

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid dehydration and prolonged immobility; individualized driving/activity restrictions after unexplained or cardiac events

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seizure: prolonged postictal confusion, lateral tongue biting; incontinence occurs in both
Hypoglycemia: persistent altered state until glucose corrected
TIA: focal deficit; isolated transient unconsciousness unusual

syncope.evidence: Not checked online; established syncope evaluation teaching.

systemic-lupus-erythematosus.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
systemic-lupus-erythematosus.scope: Diagnostic criteria (serositis, arthritis, lupus nephritis), neonatal lupus (congenital AV block), autoantibodies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith), pharmacotherapy (hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids)
systemic-lupus-erythematosus.core: Multisystem autoimmunity combining inflammatory joint, skin, serosal, renal, hematologic, or neurologic disease; flares often lower complement.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Reproductive-age women; family history; UV exposure, infections, estrogen-related triggers

rows.label: Clues
items: Photosensitive malar rash sparing nasolabial folds; painless oral ulcers; nonscarring alopecia
Symmetric nonerosive arthritis, pleuritic pain, pericarditis; leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hemolysis
★ **Proteinuria, RBC casts**, edema or hypertension → renal involvement
Neonatal lupus: maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB; congenital AV block may be permanent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-complex deposition activates **classical complement**, consuming C3/C4; autoantibody-mediated blood-cell destruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ANA** sensitive entry test; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm more specific
Anti-dsDNA titers, C3/C4, CBC, urinalysis, urine protein/creatinine, creatinine assess activity
★ Proteinuria **>0.5 g/g** or unexplained renal dysfunction → kidney biopsy
Classification: ANA ≥1:80, weighted score ≥10 with clinical criterion; clinical diagnosis remains contextual

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Hydroxychloroquine** broadly; NSAIDs for mild arthritis/serositis, glucocorticoids for flares
Organ-threatening flare → IV methylprednisolone; nephritis → mycophenolate plus belimumab/calcineurin inhibitor
Cyclophosphamide alternative for severe renal/CNS disease; taper glucocorticoids after disease control
Pregnancy → continue hydroxychloroquine; avoid mycophenolate, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Complications
items: Accelerated atherosclerosis, infection, CKD; antiphospholipid antibodies → thrombosis or pregnancy loss
Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity; chronic steroid osteoporosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Sun protection; vaccines, cardiovascular risk control, retinal monitoring
Plan pregnancy during quiescence; anti-Ro/La positivity → fetal cardiac surveillance discussion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Drug-induced lupus: antihistone antibodies, usually no renal/CNS disease
Rheumatoid arthritis: erosions; fibromyalgia: pain without inflammatory findings

systemic-vasculitis.name: Systemic vasculitis
systemic-vasculitis.scope: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (c-ANCA/PR3), microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA/MPO), eosinophilic GPA, polyarteritis nodosa, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, immunosuppressive therapy
systemic-vasculitis.core: Vessel inflammation presenting as unexplained multisystem ischemia: vessel size, organ pattern, antibodies and tissue distinguish the syndromes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; hydralazine/propylthiouracil can induce ANCA disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Constitutional symptoms, palpable purpura, skin ulcers, mononeuritis multiplex
★ **Hemoptysis + falling hemoglobin + RBC casts** → pulmonary–renal emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ANCA disease → pauci-immune necrotizing injury; larger-vessel inflammation → stenosis, thrombosis, aneurysms
Granulomas: GPA/EGPA, GCA/Takayasu; PAN: necrotizing medium-artery inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis, creatinine, CBC/differential, ESR/CRP**, chest imaging, hepatitis serologies
PR3/MPO supports diagnosis; negative ANCA cannot exclude, isolated positive cannot confirm
★ **Biopsy involved tissue**, especially kidney with GN; do not delay emergency therapy
GCA → temporal artery biopsy/expert ultrasound; **steroids before confirmation**
Takayasu → CTA/MRA; PAN → biopsy or visceral angiography showing microaneurysms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Organ-threatening disease → **urgent immunosuppression**; stabilize bleeding, renal failure, ischemia
GPA/MPA maintenance → rituximab/azathioprine; methotrexate if renal function permits
Plasma exchange not routine in ANCA; consider severe renal disease/anti-GBM overlap
GCA steroid sparing → tocilizumab; elective vascular reconstruction after inflammation controlled
HCV cryoglobulinemia → **direct-acting antivirals**, not immunosuppression alone; older questions may expect interferon-alfa

rows.label: Complications
items: Blindness, renal failure, stroke, bowel infarction, aortic aneurysm
Cyclophosphamide → infertility/cystitis/malignancy; rituximab → HBV reactivation; steroids → infection/osteoporosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **TMP-SMX** with cyclophosphamide/rituximab induction; HBV/TB testing before biologics
Vaccination, bone protection, fertility counseling; follow clinical findings, not ANCA titers alone

rows.label: Mimics
items: Endocarditis: positive blood cultures/vegetations; ANCA sometimes positive
Anti-GBM: linear IgG on renal biopsy
Cholesterol emboli: vascular procedure, blue toes, eosinophilia, preserved pulses

table.title: Disease signatures
rows: PR3/c-ANCA; destructive sinonasal/ear disease, cavitary lungs, GN
Severe disease: same induction as GPA
Steroids; severe → cyclophosphamide; nonsevere relapsing → mepolizumab
Age >50; jaw claudication, visual symptoms, PMR
Young women; pulse/BP discrepancy, arm claudication

testicular-torsion.name: Testicular torsion
testicular-torsion.scope: Testicular torsion, absent cremasteric reflex, bell-clapper deformity, Doppler ultrasound, surgical detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
testicular-torsion.core: Sudden unilateral scrotal pain with vomiting in an adolescent is spermatic cord torsion until excluded; salvage depends on immediate action.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Bell-clapper deformity permits excessive intravaginal rotation; often bilateral anatomic predisposition
Pubertal peak; may follow sleep, activity, or minor trauma; neonates can have extravaginal torsion

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **High-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex**, diffuse tenderness and swelling
Pain may present as lower abdominal discomfort without volunteered scrotal symptoms
Prior self-resolving attacks suggest intermittent torsion; symptom resolution does not eliminate recurrence risk
Delayed fever/erythema can occur; no single examination finding reliably excludes torsion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cord rotation obstructs venous drainage then arterial inflow → progressive ischemia
Viability falls rapidly with delay; greatest salvage when detorsion occurs within about 6 hours

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ High clinical suspicion → **immediate urologic exploration**, no imaging delay
Equivocal presentation → **color Doppler ultrasound**, comparing perfusion with opposite testis
Reduced/absent flow or twisted cord supports diagnosis; preserved flow possible in partial/intermittent torsion
Urinalysis for infection if uncertain; pyuria does not automatically exclude simultaneous torsion
Examine both testes in boys with unexplained acute abdominal pain; ultrasound cannot overrule compelling clinical findings

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Urgent surgical detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy**; orchiectomy only if nonviable
NPO, IV analgesia, fluids as needed; call urology while preparing operation
★ If surgical delay unavoidable → **manual outward detorsion** as bridge; direction sometimes reversed
Pain relief after manual detorsion still requires operative confirmation and fixation; residual twisting possible

rows.label: Complications
items: Infarction, testicular loss, later atrophy, reduced fertility; endocrine function often maintained by opposite testis
Reperfusion does not guarantee long-term viability; follow-up for atrophy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Contralateral fixation addresses shared anatomy; evaluate recurrent episodic scrotal pain promptly
Teach adolescents to report sudden pain immediately despite embarrassment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Epididymitis: gradual pain, urinary/STI symptoms, increased epididymal Doppler flow
Appendix testis torsion: focal superior-pole tenderness, blue-dot sign, preserved testicular flow
Incarcerated hernia: irreducible inguinoscrotal mass, possible bowel obstruction

testicular-torsion.evidence: Not checked online; established urologic emergency assessment and salvage principles.

thoracic-trauma.name: Thoracic trauma
thoracic-trauma.scope: Blunt and penetrating chest trauma, blunt cardiac injury, blunt aortic injury, diaphragmatic rupture, pulmonary contusion
thoracic-trauma.core: Chest trauma with respiratory or circulatory compromise requires immediate treatment of life-threatening injuries before definitive imaging.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, steering-wheel impact, crush injuries, penetrating wounds
Lower chest wounds can cross diaphragm and injure abdominal organs

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral absent breath sounds, shock, distended neck veins → tension pneumothorax
Flail segment: paradoxical movement; associated lung injury drives hypoxemia
Hypoxemia hours after impact + focal alveolar infiltrate, worsening to 24–48 h, afebrile → **pulmonary contusion**
Left thoracic bowel sounds/loops, **NG tip in left chest**, obscured hemidiaphragm → diaphragmatic rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pleural pressure or pericardial blood impairs venous return → obstructive shock
Alveolar hemorrhage and edema impair gas exchange; rapid deceleration shears the aortic isthmus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Primary survey with **eFAST** and portable chest radiograph; unstable injuries treated clinically
★ Deceleration + **widened mediastinum** → aortic injury; stable → **CT angiography**; normal radiograph cannot exclude
Blunt cardiac injury → ECG and troponin; both normal effectively exclude significant injury
Sternal/anterior rib fractures + new arrhythmia/↑troponin → telemetry; persistent shock → echocardiography
Large persistent air leak, subcutaneous air despite working chest tube → **tracheobronchial rupture**; bronchoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle/finger decompression → **chest tube**; no imaging delay
Open pneumothorax → vented seal and tube; hemothorax → tube and blood resuscitation
★ Initial tube blood >1500 mL or persistent >200 mL/h → operative exploration
Tamponade with shock/arrest → surgical drainage; pericardiocentesis only temporizing
Contusion/flail chest → oxygen, regional/multimodal analgesia, pulmonary hygiene; intubate for respiratory failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Contusion → ARDS; retained hemothorax → empyema
Rib fractures → splinting, atelectasis, pneumonia; cardiac injury → arrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, vehicle safety systems and protective equipment reduce injury risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Myocardial contusion: ventricular ectopy, rising wedge pressure, pulmonary edema after fluids; no pericardial compression
Abdominal hemorrhage: free intraperitoneal fluid; may coexist with thoracic injury
Massive hemothorax: **opacified hemithorax**, flat neck veins; tension pneumothorax: hyperlucent
ARDS: bilateral opacities after 24–48 h; fat embolism: long-bone fracture, petechiae, confusion

thoracic-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established ATLS-based teaching.

table.title: Definitive associated-injury management
rows: IV esmolol if tolerated; endovascular repair

toxic-alcohol-poisoning.name: Toxic alcohol poisoning
toxic-alcohol-poisoning.scope: Ethylene glycol (calcium oxalate, renal failure), methanol (visual impairment, optic disc hyperemia), isopropyl alcohol (ketosis without acidosis), osmolar gap, fomepizole, hemodialysis
toxic-alcohol-poisoning.core: Unexplained intoxication with an osmolar gap suggests toxic alcohol exposure; delayed organic-acid accumulation can produce profound anion-gap acidosis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Antifreeze, windshield-washer fluid, solvents; accidental ingestion or self-harm; substitute alcohol consumption

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting, abdominal pain, altered consciousness; tachypnea or shock signals severe toxicity
★ **Normal osmolar gap does not exclude late poisoning**; history may be unavailable

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts parent alcohols into characteristic metabolites
Parent compounds elevate osmolar gap early; metabolites later raise anion gap in acid-producing ingestions

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Electrolytes, ABG/VBG, glucose, BUN, measured osmolality, ethanol and specific alcohol levels
Calculated osmolality = 2Na + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; add ethanol/4.6, concentrations in mg/dL
Measured minus calculated >10 mOsm/kg supports exposure; nonspecific and time-dependent
Urinalysis and calcium/creatinine assess organ injury; absent characteristic sediment inclusions do not exclude exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway, IV fluids, poison-center consultation; **fomepizole** immediately for suspected methanol/ethylene glycol
Methanol: vision loss, coma/seizures or pH ≤7.15 → **hemodialysis**; ethylene glycol: severe acidosis/AKI → dialysis
Sodium bicarbonate for marked acidemia; methanol → folinic acid; ethylene glycol → thiamine/pyridoxine adjuncts
★ Isopropanol → supportive care; **avoid fomepizole**, which prolongs parent-compound toxicity

rows.label: Complications
items: Methanol: permanent blindness, basal ganglia injury
Oxalate toxicity: hypocalcemic dysrhythmias; any ingestion: aspiration, coma, death

rows.label: Prevention
items: Store products separately from beverages; child-resistant containers; suicide-risk assessment after intentional ingestion

rows.label: Mimics
items: DKA: hyperglycemia and β-hydroxybutyrate elevation
Alcoholic ketoacidosis: poor intake after alcohol binge, low/normal glucose

toxic-alcohol-poisoning.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [EXTRIP methanol](https://www.extrip-workgroup.org/methanol), [ethylene glycol](https://www.extrip-workgroup.org/ethylene-glycol); other principles: established toxicology teaching.

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis
tuberculosis.scope: Latent TB infection screening (PPD, IGRA), treatment regimens, active pulmonary TB, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, RIPE therapy, extrapulmonary TB (Pott disease)
tuberculosis.core: Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe cavitation suggest contagious pulmonary tuberculosis; latent infection has no active disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Close contact, endemic residence, incarceration, homelessness, crowding, **long-term care** work/volunteering
HIV, TNF inhibitors, transplant, silicosis, diabetes → progression/reactivation risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Hemoptysis, prolonged fever; primary disease may cause hilar adenopathy or pleural effusion
★ **Back pain with vertebral destruction** → Pott disease; miliary spread causes diffuse micronodules
Tuberculous pleurisy: **lymphocytic exudate**, high protein, low glucose

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airborne bacilli survive in macrophages; T-cell granulomas contain infection; T-cell dysfunction → reactivation, skin-test anergy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screening: **IGRA** preferred after BCG; TST read induration at 48–72 hours
Positive screening → symptoms + chest radiograph; neither test distinguishes latent from active infection
★ Active suspicion → **sputum NAAT, AFB smear, culture and susceptibility**; collect serial specimens
Negative smear, TST or IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially with immunosuppression or malnutrition
Pott suspicion → spinal MRI, biopsy/culture; assess cord compression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected contagious disease → **airborne isolation** and public-health notification
Drug-susceptible active TB: 2 months isoniazid/rifampin/pyrazinamide/ethambutol → 4 months isoniazid/rifampin
Eligible pulmonary cases ≥12 years: 4-month isoniazid/rifapentine/moxifloxacin/pyrazinamide-based regimen alternative
Latent, no RIPE: 3-month isoniazid/rifapentine or 4-month rifampin; older questions may expect **isoniazid** alone, still acceptable
Isoniazid → pyridoxine prevents neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia; Pott with deficit/instability → urgent spinal surgery evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Meningitis, adrenal destruction, spinal cord compression, bronchiectasis
INH/rifampin/pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity; ethambutol: optic neuropathy; rifampin: enzyme induction, orange secretions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Contact investigation**, latent-treatment completion; directly observed active treatment improves adherence
Review drug interactions and baseline liver risk; monitor visual acuity/color vision with ethambutol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung cancer: focal malignant biopsy
Fungal infection: geographic exposure; nontuberculous mycobacteria: species identification distinguishes

table.title: Positive TST thresholds
rows: HIV, close contacts, transplant, substantial immunosuppression
Healthcare workers, exposure-risk groups, comorbidities, young children

type-2-diabetes-mellitus.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
type-2-diabetes-mellitus.scope: Diagnosis, glycemic targets, pharmacotherapy (metformin contraindications, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA, insulin), chronic complications screening, pediatric screening in obesity
type-2-diabetes-mellitus.core: Insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure produces chronic hyperglycemia and vascular injury, often preceding obvious symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central obesity, family history, prior gestational diabetes, PCOS, physical inactivity
Glucocorticoids and atypical antipsychotics can unmask dysglycemia

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria, polydipsia, blurred vision, recurrent candidiasis; acanthosis nigricans suggests marked insulin resistance
Weight loss, ketosis, or dehydration → severe insulin deficiency; reconsider diabetes type

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired glucose uptake + excess hepatic output; early compensatory **↑serum insulin**, later relative secretory failure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **A1c ≥6.5%**, fasting glucose ≥126, or 2-hour OGTT ≥200 mg/dL
Random glucose ≥200 with classic symptoms also diagnostic; otherwise confirm with second abnormal result
A1c unreliable with altered erythrocyte survival; use plasma glucose
★ Youth: screen puberty/age 10, whichever earlier, with overweight/obesity + additional risk; repeat ≥every 2 years

rows.label: Tx
items: Lifestyle + metformin; **lactic acidosis**: avoid eGFR <30, AKI/sepsis, hypoxia; no new start <45; reduce 30–44
★ HF/CKD → **SGLT2 inhibitor**; ASCVD/obesity → GLP-1 RA, independent of A1c or metformin
★ Catabolism, glucose ≥300, or A1c >10% → **insulin**
Otherwise GLP-1 RA before insulin; older exam questions may expect **basal insulin** once two orals fail
Adults: A1c <7%, fasting 80–130, postmeal <180; relax for frailty/hypoglycemia; quarterly checks until stable

rows.label: Complications
items: Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, foot ulceration; coronary, cerebral, and peripheral arterial disease
SGLT2 inhibitors: genital mycoses, euglycemic DKA; sulfonylureas/insulin: hypoglycemia, weight gain
Metformin: GI intolerance, B12 deficiency; pioglitazone: edema, HF; sulfonylureas: labeled caution with sulfa allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ At diagnosis then annually: **urine albumin/creatinine, eGFR, foot and dilated eye examinations** (eye spacing by findings)
★ Albuminuria + hypertension → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**, never both; efferent dilation ↓intraglomerular pressure
BP ≥130/80 → antihypertensive; older exam questions may expect ACE inhibitor, also normotensive albuminuria
Statin age 40–75; glycemic control slows **neuropathy**, retinopathy, nephropathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Type 1 diabetes: autoantibodies, low C-peptide, abrupt ketosis
Diabetes insipidus: dilute polyuria without elevated blood glucose

urinary-incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
urinary-incontinence.core: Involuntary urine leakage is classified by triggers, urgency, bladder emptying, and ability to reach a toilet; reversible contributors often coexist.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childbirth, pelvic surgery, aging, obesity; diabetes, neurologic disease, prostate enlargement
Diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics, constipation, infection, impaired mobility/cognition worsen control

rows.label: Clues
items: History: timing, volume, dysuria, weak stream, nocturia, fluid intake, obstetric/surgical and neurologic history
★ **New saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, retention** → urgent cauda equina evaluation
Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery/radiation suggests fistula; recurrent UTIs/hematuria require further investigation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stress: aging/multiparity weaken pelvic floor → **urethral hypermobility**, low sphincter tone
Urge: **uninhibited detrusor contractions** (detrusor instability), worsened by caffeine; MS lesion → low residual
Overflow: **detrusor underactivity/acontractile bladder** (MS, diabetes, stroke) or outlet obstruction → high residual
Functional impairment can prevent continence despite intact lower urinary tract function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis + voiding diary**, focused pelvic/prostate and neurologic examination; review medications
Cough stress test with reasonably full bladder; assess prolapse, atrophy, fecal impaction
**Q-tip excursion >30°** on Valsalva → urethral hypermobility (urethrocele)
★ Suspected retention/emptying symptoms → **postvoid residual**; persistent >200 mL suggests inadequate emptying
No routine initial urodynamics/cystoscopy; uncertainty, hematuria, refractory symptoms → additional testing

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat reversible contributor; mixed incontinence → target most bothersome component
★ **Pelvic floor training/bladder training** underpin conservative care; weight loss, reduce caffeine, timed voiding
Urgency drugs: mirabegron or antimuscarinic (oxybutynin); discuss cognitive risk and avoid antimuscarinics with retention
Mirabegron may increase BP; avoid severe uncontrolled hypertension; refractory urgency → botulinum toxin or neuromodulation
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause → local vaginal estrogen when suitable; not systemic estrogen for leakage

rows.label: Complications
items: Dermatitis, falls from rushing, social isolation, sleep disruption
Overflow → hydronephrosis/renal injury; bladder botulinum toxin → retention, UTI

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication review, accessible toilet, mobility aids; bowel regularity, maintain strength and weight

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polyuria: high urine volume from hyperglycemia/diuresis rather than primary storage failure
Vaginal fistula: constant leakage unrelated to voiding urge or exertion

valvular-heart-disease.name: Valvular heart disease
valvular-heart-disease.scope: Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, physical exam, echocardiography, surgical and transcatheter replacement
valvular-heart-disease.core: Murmur timing, location, radiation, and loading maneuvers localize valve disease; symptoms and ventricular response determine intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trileaflet calcification, age >70 → AS; rheumatic disease → MS
Bicuspid valve: murmur from youth, premature calcific AS (40s–60s); childhood **endocarditis**; adult aortic dissection
AR: endocarditis, dissection, **root dilation** (Marfan, hypertension; murmur along right sternal border)
MR: ischemia, myxomatous prolapse (connective tissue laxity), chamber dilation

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, pulmonary edema, reduced exercise tolerance; abrupt deterioration suggests acute regurgitation
★ **Exertional syncope, angina, or HF** with obstruction → severe symptomatic disease
Squatting/handgrip increase regurgitant murmurs; standing/Valsalva → earlier MVP click, squatting → later

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stenosis produces upstream pressure overload; regurgitation produces chamber volume overload
Acute regurgitation lacks compensatory dilation, rapidly elevating filling pressures and reducing forward output
Mitral stenosis: ↑LA pressure, ↑PCWP, ↑pulmonary artery pressure; **LVEDP normal**; AF abolishes presystolic accentuation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TTE Doppler** defines anatomy, severity, EF, chamber dimensions, pulmonary pressures
Severe AS: velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40, or valve area ≤1 cm²; discordance requires reassessment
Severe MS: valve area ≤1.5 cm²; TEE for thrombus before balloon intervention or uncertain anatomy
★ Acute murmur with shock → **urgent echocardiography**; TEE if endocarditis/dissection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe AR/MR → **urgent surgery**, stabilize with afterload reduction/diuresis if BP permits
Severe primary MR: **EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm** triggers intervention even without symptoms
